    # Me Home AI — Demo-first product
    
    Me Home AI is a privacy-first home agentic system. This is its first product release:
    a public product website and an interactive demo that shows the intended experience.
    The demo is a product showcase, not a production home-control application.
    Learn about the vision at [Me — Your intelligence. Yours.](https://mehomeai.replit.app/me/).
    
    ## Development
    
    This is a pnpm workspace using Node.js 24 and TypeScript. Install dependencies with
    `pnpm install`, then run `pnpm run typecheck` or `pnpm run build` from the repository
    root (the build command expects `PORT` and `BASE_PATH`). Run the website with
    `PORT=5000 BASE_PATH=/ pnpm --filter @workspace/web dev` and the interactive demo
    with `PORT=5001 BASE_PATH=/ pnpm --filter @workspace/demo dev`.
    
    ## Repository layout
    
    - `apps/web` — public product website and waitlist experience.
    - `apps/demo` — interactive, video-based product demo.
    - `packages/api-server` — API used by the website waitlist.
    - `packages/api-client-react`, `packages/api-spec`, `packages/api-zod`, `packages/db` —
      shared API contracts, generated clients/validators, and database schema.
    - `tools/mockup-sandbox` — development-only mockup preview tool, not part of the product.
    - `scripts` — workspace utilities.
    
    The waitlist API requires `DATABASE_URL` to connect to PostgreSQL. See `replit.md` and the
    workspace package scripts for additional development commands.
    
    ## Contributing
    
    Start with the [contribution guide](https://github.com/mehomeai/.github/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md),
    [code of conduct](https://github.com/mehomeai/.github/blob/main/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md), and
    [governance](https://github.com/mehomeai/.github/blob/main/GOVERNANCE.md).
    Discuss substantial changes in an issue before implementing them. Pull requests
    should include relevant tests and documentation.
    
    For questions and cross-project planning, use [community discussions](https://github.com/mehomeai/.github/discussions).
    Report vulnerabilities privately through this repository's **Security → Report a vulnerability**;
    see the [security policy](https://github.com/mehomeai/.github/blob/main/SECURITY.md).

    import { type ReactNode } from 'react';
    import { QueryClient, QueryClientProvider } from '@tanstack/react-query';
    import { ErrorBoundary } from '@/components/error-boundary';
    import { Toaster } from '@/components/ui/toaster';
    import { TooltipProvider } from '@/components/ui/tooltip';
    import NotFound from '@/pages/not-found';
    import Home from '@/pages/home';
    import HowItWorks from '@/pages/how-it-works';
    import Signup from '@/pages/signup';
    import { PageMetadata } from '@/components/page-metadata';
    import {
      Route,
      Switch,
      useLocation,
      Router as WouterRouter,
    } from 'wouter';
    
    const queryClient = new QueryClient();
    
    function Router() {
      return (
        // Keep a shared shell (sidebar, navbar) outside the boundary so it
        // survives a page crash.
        <RoutedErrorBoundary>
          <Switch>
            <Route path="/" component={Home} />
            <Route path="/how-it-works" component={HowItWorks} />
            <Route path="/signup" component={Signup} />
            <Route component={NotFound} />
          </Switch>
        </RoutedErrorBoundary>
      );
    }
    
    function RoutedErrorBoundary({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
      const [location] = useLocation();
      return <ErrorBoundary resetKey={location}>{children}</ErrorBoundary>;
    }
    
    function App() {
      return (
        <QueryClientProvider client={queryClient}>
          <TooltipProvider>
            <WouterRouter base={import.meta.env.BASE_URL.replace(/\/$/, '')}>
              <PageMetadata />
              <Router />
            </WouterRouter>
            <Toaster />
          </TooltipProvider>
        </QueryClientProvider>
      );
    }
    
    export default App;

          <p className="mt-6 text-xs leading-relaxed text-muted-foreground">Illustrative control. You set what the feed optimizes for. Not watch time.</p>

    import { useState } from 'react';
    import { useForm } from 'react-hook-form';
    import { Link } from 'wouter';
    import { motion } from 'framer-motion';

    import { useJoinMeWaitlist } from '@workspace/api-client-react';
    import { ConceptLabel, EASE, MeMark, SiteShell, img } from '@/components/site';
    
    type FormValues = { email: string; consent: boolean; website: string };
    
    function errorMessage(err: unknown): string {
      const e = err as { data?: { error?: string; message?: string }; message?: string } | null;
      return e?.data?.error || e?.data?.message || 'Something went wrong. Please try again.';
    }
    
    export default function Signup() {
      const join = useJoinMeWaitlist();
      const [done, setDone] = useState<string | null>(null);
      const [serverError, setServerError] = useState<string | null>(null);
      const { register, handleSubmit, formState: { errors } } = useForm<FormValues>({
        defaultValues: { email: '', consent: false, website: '' },
      });
    
      const onSubmit = (v: FormValues) => {
        setServerError(null);
        join.mutate(
          { data: { email: v.email.trim(), consent: true, ...(v.website ? { website: v.website } : {}) } },
          {
            onSuccess: (r) => { if (r.success) setDone(r.message); else setServerError(r.message || 'We could not add you. Please try again.'); },
            onError: (e) => setServerError(errorMessage(e)),
          },
        );
      };
    
      return (
        <SiteShell>
          <section className="mx-auto grid max-w-6xl gap-12 px-5 pt-14 md:grid-cols-[1.1fr_1fr] md:px-8 md:pt-24">
            <div>
              <div className="eyebrow">Waitlist</div>
              <h1 className="f-display mt-5 text-[clamp(44px,7vw,88px)] leading-[0.98]">Hear when<br /><span className="text-accent">Me is ready.</span></h1>
              <p className="mt-6 max-w-md text-lg leading-relaxed text-muted-foreground">One email address. Launch updates only. This is a waitlist, not an account.</p>
    
              <div className="mt-10 max-w-md rounded-3xl border border-border bg-card p-6 md:p-8">
                {done ? (
                  <motion.div initial={{ opacity: 0, y: 10 }} animate={{ opacity: 1, y: 0 }} transition={{ duration: 0.5, ease: EASE }} data-testid="status-success">
                    <div className="grid h-11 w-11 place-items-center rounded-full bg-accent text-accent-foreground"><Check className="h-5 w-5" /></div>
                    <div className="f-display mt-5 text-3xl">You're on the list.</div>
                    <p className="mt-2 text-muted-foreground" data-testid="text-success-message">{done}</p>
                    <Link href="/how-it-works" className="mt-6 inline-flex items-center gap-2 text-sm text-accent hover:underline" data-testid="link-success-how">Read how it works <ArrowRight className="h-4 w-4" /></Link>
                  </motion.div>
                ) : (
                  <form onSubmit={handleSubmit(onSubmit)} noValidate>
                    <label htmlFor="email" className="text-sm font-medium">Email</label>
                    <input id="email" type="email" autoComplete="email" placeholder="you@example.com" disabled={join.isPending}
                      {...register('email', { required: 'Enter your email address.', maxLength: { value: 254, message: 'That email is too long.' }, pattern: { value: /^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]+$/, message: 'Enter a valid email address.' } })}
                      className="mt-2 w-full rounded-xl border border-input bg-background px-4 py-3 text-base outline-none transition focus:border-accent focus:ring-2 focus:ring-accent/20"
                      data-testid="input-email" />
                    {errors.email && <p className="mt-2 text-sm text-destructive" data-testid="error-email">{errors.email.message}</p>}
    
                    <div aria-hidden className="absolute -left-[9999px] h-0 w-0 overflow-hidden">
                      <label htmlFor="website">Website</label>
                      <input id="website" tabIndex={-1} autoComplete="off" {...register('website')} />
                    </div>
    
                    <label className="mt-5 flex cursor-pointer gap-3 text-sm leading-relaxed text-muted-foreground">
                      <input type="checkbox" disabled={join.isPending} {...register('consent', { validate: (v) => v || 'Please confirm to join the waitlist.' })}
                        className="mt-1 h-4 w-4 shrink-0 accent-[#1e6b66]" data-testid="checkbox-consent" />
                      <span>I agree to have my email stored by this website so the Me team can send me launch updates.</span>
                    </label>
                    {errors.consent && <p className="mt-2 text-sm text-destructive" data-testid="error-consent">{errors.consent.message}</p>}
    
                    {serverError && <p className="mt-4 rounded-xl border border-destructive/30 bg-destructive/5 px-4 py-3 text-sm text-destructive" role="alert" data-testid="status-error">{serverError}</p>}
    
                    <button type="submit" disabled={join.isPending} className="mt-6 inline-flex w-full items-center justify-center gap-2 rounded-full bg-primary px-6 py-3.5 text-sm text-primary-foreground transition-opacity hover:opacity-85 disabled:opacity-60" data-testid="button-submit">
                      {join.isPending ? <><Loader2 className="h-4 w-4 animate-spin" /> Joining</> : <>Join the waitlist <ArrowRight className="h-4 w-4" /></>}
                    </button>
                  </form>
                )}
              </div>
              <p className="mt-5 max-w-md text-xs leading-relaxed text-muted-foreground">
                Note: your waitlist email is sent to and stored on this website's server. That is separate from Me's private chat, which is processed and stored on Me Home.
              </p>
            </div>
    
            <div className="relative hidden overflow-hidden rounded-3xl md:block">
              <img src={img('me-home-room.jpg')} alt="Concept render of Me Home in a living room" className="h-full w-full object-cover" />
              <ConceptLabel className="absolute bottom-5 right-5" />
              <div className="absolute left-6 top-6 flex items-center gap-2 rounded-full bg-card/90 px-3 py-1.5 backdrop-blur"><MeMark size={16} /><span className="f-mono text-[10px] text-accent">ME HOME · LIVING ROOM</span></div>
            </div>
          </section>
        </SiteShell>
      );
    }
    import { Router, type IRouter } from "express";
    import { db, meWaitlistTable } from "@workspace/db";
    import { JoinMeWaitlistBody, JoinMeWaitlistResponse } from "@workspace/api-zod";
    
    const router: IRouter = Router();
    const attempts = new Map<string, { count: number; resetAt: number }>();
    const windowMs = 15 * 60 * 1000;
    const receipt = JoinMeWaitlistResponse.parse({
      success: true,
      message: "You're on the list. We'll share Me launch updates with you.",
    });
    
    router.post("/me/waitlist", async (req, res): Promise<void> => {
      res.setHeader("Cache-Control", "no-store");
      const now = Date.now();
      for (const [key, value] of attempts) {
        if (value.resetAt <= now) attempts.delete(key);
      }
      // Include the address so visitors behind the shared reverse proxy do not
      // consume one another's signup allowance. Never persist the network address.
      const emailKey = typeof req.body?.email === "string"
        ? req.body.email.trim().toLowerCase().slice(0, 254)
        : "invalid";
      const key = `${req.ip ?? "unknown"}:${emailKey}`;
      const attempt = attempts.get(key);
      if (attempt && attempt.count >= 15) {
        res.setHeader("Retry-After", Math.ceil((attempt.resetAt - now) / 1000));
        res.status(429).json({ error: "Too many attempts. Please try again later." });
        return;
      }
      if (attempt) attempt.count += 1;
      else if (attempts.size < 10000) attempts.set(key, { count: 1, resetAt: now + windowMs });
      else {
        res.status(429).json({ error: "Too many attempts. Please try again later." });
        return;
      }
    
      const input = req.body && typeof req.body === "object"
        ? { ...req.body, email: typeof req.body.email === "string" ? req.body.email.trim().toLowerCase() : req.body.email }
        : req.body;
      const parsed = JoinMeWaitlistBody.safeParse(input);
      if (!parsed.success || parsed.data.consent !== true) {
        res.status(400).json({ error: "Enter a valid email and agree to receive Me launch updates." });
        return;
      }
      if (parsed.data.website) {
        res.json(receipt);
        return;
      }
      try {
        await db.insert(meWaitlistTable).values({
          email: parsed.data.email,
          consentVersion: "launch-updates-v1",
        }).onConflictDoNothing({ target: meWaitlistTable.email });
        res.json(receipt);
      } catch (err) {
        req.log.error({ err }, "Me waitlist signup failed");
        res.status(503).json({ error: "We couldn't save your signup. Please try again shortly." });
      }
    });
    
    export default router;

I’ve read the main pages, demo structure, and waitlist API.

**Me is a family-owned AI system:** a dedicated **Me Home** computer runs local models and stores household memory, while the **Me** phone app connects family members to it.

The core experience is:

- **Private chat:** conversations and personal context stay on the home computer.
- **A family-controlled feed:** parents tune content toward learning and goals.
- **Permissioned actions:** tasks like price checks or bookings request approval before sharing the required information.
- **Household rules:** parents manage children’s access and supervise usage.

The current `web-app` is a **prelaunch website and animated product showcase**. It has overview, how-it-works, and waitlist pages; the waitlist saves consented emails to PostgreSQL. The chat, hardware, and family controls shown here illustrate the intended product.

The central promise: **your family owns the intelligence, its data, and its rules.**

    #!/usr/bin/env python3
    """Check the bootstrap repository contract and accidental credential file commits.
    
    This is repository hygiene, not application validation or a full secret scanner.
    """
    from pathlib import Path
    import subprocess
    import sys
    
    required = ('README.md', 'LICENSE', '.github/CODEOWNERS', '.github/workflows/ci.yml')
    errors = [f'Missing or empty file: {name}' for name in required
              if not Path(name).is_file() or not Path(name).read_text().strip()]
    tracked = subprocess.check_output(['git', 'ls-files', '-z']).decode().split('\0')
    for name in filter(None, tracked):
        p = Path(name)
        if p.name == '.env' or (p.name.startswith('.env.') and
                                p.suffix not in ('.example', '.sample', '.template')):
            errors.append(f'Remove tracked environment secrets file: {name}')
        if p.name in ('id_rsa', 'id_ed25519') or p.suffix in ('.p12', '.pfx', '.key'):
            errors.append(f'Remove tracked private key file: {name}')
        try:
            content = p.read_text()
        except (UnicodeDecodeError, OSError):
            continue
        if any(line.startswith(('<<<<<<< ', '>>>>>>> ')) for line in content.splitlines()):
            errors.append(f'Unresolved merge conflict: {name}')
    if errors:
        print('\n'.join(errors), file=sys.stderr)
        sys.exit(1)
    print('Repository health checks passed. Add application tests when code is introduced.')

    # Me personal agent: architecture and delivery plan
    
    Status: proposed implementation plan; no runtime has been implemented or benchmarked.
    Research date: 2026-11-02. Framework claims below come from linked upstream documentation; recommendations, estimates, and acceptance targets are Me design proposals.
    
    ## 1. Product and starting point
    
    Build a persistent personal agent on Me Home that can understand requests, use tools, produce useful artifacts, remember authorized context, and continue work after the phone disconnects. The same agent should handle household assistance, research, browser tasks, coding/debugging, and animation creation through capability modules.
    
    The inspected `agentic-framework`, `backend-server`, `infra-server`, and `phone-app` repositories contain bootstrap documentation and hygiene checks, rather than application implementations. `web-app` contains the public website, a scripted animated showcase, and a waitlist API. Its phone mockups are not an existing agent client.
    
    The product contract established by the website is local private inference and storage, household-controlled access, and permission before contacting external services. The first real agent must preserve that contract.
    
    First release scope: a developer/household alpha on a single Me Home, with a thin client and a documented hardware configuration. A reliable consumer appliance, broad desktop automation, and unrestricted autonomous purchasing require subsequent releases.
    
    The references “OpenAI dot,” “Muse,” and “grokbot” are unresolved project names pending exact URLs. They are not treated as verified candidates or silently mapped to other projects.
    
    ## 2. Recommended reuse strategy
    
    **Provisional choice: embed Deep Agents as the agent harness, use its LangGraph runtime, and build Me's household control layer around it.** Install pinned upstream packages and extend documented interfaces. Avoid maintaining a fork unless an evaluation reveals a concrete blocker.
    
    [Deep Agents](https://github.com/langchain-ai/deepagents) provides planning-oriented execution, filesystem backends, context management, skills, subagents, and human review support. It is MIT-licensed and supports tool-calling models, including local models. These are upstream features, not evidence of Me task quality. [LangGraph persistence](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/persistence) and [interrupts](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/interrupts) provide the primitives for persisted execution and approval pauses.
    
    Me should own identity, household rules, memory authorization, tool execution permissions, task records, artifacts, and the phone-facing contract. These remain stable if the harness changes. The framework's default filesystem, shell, delegation, and memory tools must be replaced or constrained through Me-controlled adapters; wrapping only newly added tools is insufficient.
    
    Use one general agent initially. Select capabilities and skills according to the task. Add isolated specialist workers when a workflow needs a separate environment or when evaluation demonstrates a benefit. Default to serial execution on a home device; explicitly budget parallel workers.
    
    ### Alternatives and their intended roles
    
    | Foundation | What upstream supplies | Proposed role and decision condition |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | [Deep Agents + LangGraph](https://github.com/langchain-ai/deepagents) | Embeddable harness and persisted runtime | Preferred product foundation, subject to the evaluation below. Me supplies household controls and execution isolation. |
    | [Hermes Agent](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent) | Personal assistant with memory, skills, scheduling, terminal backends, and configurable model endpoints; MIT | Best full-assistant challenger for the alpha. Choose it if its integration surface preserves all Me controls with substantially less engineering. Review automatic skill updates and every optional external memory/service integration. |
    | [OpenClaw](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw) | Self-hosted assistant gateway, channels, tools, and swappable model integrations; MIT | Strong full-product challenger, especially if messaging channels become central. Evaluate an isolated per-user deployment rather than assuming its shared gateway meets Me's family privacy requirements. |
    | [nanobot](https://github.com/HKUDS/nanobot) | Smaller Python personal-agent implementation with memory, scheduling, local endpoints, and MCP; MIT | Lightweight baseline and fallback if device resources or integration complexity rule out larger candidates. Test recovery and authorization rather than inferring them from feature lists. |
    | [LangGraph directly](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph) | Lower-level orchestration runtime; MIT | Fallback if the opinionated harness creates persistent policy or context-management problems. Requires building more of the agent loop. |
    | [OpenHands Software Agent SDK](https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk) | Embeddable coding agents, tools, workspace execution, and server APIs; MIT | Optional coding worker, not a second household orchestrator. Add only if the initial coding capability misses its quality target. |
    
    OpenClaw documents [one trusted boundary per gateway](https://docs.openclaw.ai/gateway/security). It also documents host execution for the main session unless sandboxing is configured. This is an integration constraint, not a claim that OpenClaw is unsuitable for every household deployment.
    
    No framework supplies all of Me's product guarantees automatically. “Runs locally” describes deployment; it does not establish that model calls, tracing, plugins, or tools remain local.
    
    ### One-week selection experiment
    
    1. Freeze a 30-task fixture set before tuning: six each for personal memory/documents, browsing, coding/debugging, animation/artifacts, and recovery/permissions. Add separate adversarial permission tests.
    2. Pin releases/commit identifiers, dependency locks, model revision, quantization, prompts, tool set, and device configuration. Record licenses and optional service dependencies. Research currently describes upstream main branches; the experiment must select actual releases.
    3. Compare Deep Agents, Hermes, and OpenClaw on identical tasks and local model endpoints. Use nanobot as a small-footprint baseline only if capacity permits; do not delay the decision for exhaustive framework coverage.
    4. Spend equal, capped integration time on each. Record unsupported adapters as integration cost rather than silently giving candidates unequal tools.
    5. Eliminate candidates that cannot enforce the tool broker, isolate user data, run without unapproved external calls, or pause/recover safely. Score remaining candidates: task correctness 35%, local latency/resource use 20%, integration effort 20%, recovery 15%, dependency/maintenance burden 10%.
    6. Report task-level outcomes and repeat the leading candidates three times. A small fixture set supports an engineering choice, not a universal performance claim.
    7. Write an architecture decision record with measured results, upstream versions, known failures, and the chosen foundation. If no local model passes, narrow the supported alpha workflows and rerun; do not silently enable cloud inference.
    
    ## 3. User-visible workflows
    
    | Workflow | End-to-end behavior | Evidence of completion |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | Personal assistance | Answer from the user's allowed files and memories; ask before adding ambiguous or sensitive durable memories | Answer cites the local source; saved memory is inspectable, correctable, and deletable |
    | Research | Obtain scoped external access, browse allowed sources, synthesize findings, and save a report | Source links, retrieval timestamps, and report artifact |
    | Browser task | Navigate an isolated user browser, inspect state, fill a draft, and pause before an external commitment | Page evidence plus approval and resulting confirmation, or an explicit blocked result |
    | Code/debug | Create a task workspace, inspect code, edit, execute tests, use failure output, and repair within a bounded loop | Patch/source, test results, and runnable local preview where applicable |
    | Animation | Convert a brief to scenes and code, render a preview, inspect frames, revise, and export | Editable source, playable output, render logs, and checks of duration/resolution/content |
    | Recurring task | User explicitly creates a schedule with an allowed capability and scope; scheduler starts a normal persisted run | Inspectable schedule, execution history, cancel control, and approval pause where needed |
    
    Example acceptance story: “Create a 20-second animation explaining fractions for Maya.” The agent uses the authorized child profile, creates a storyboard and Manim source, renders locally, checks frames and duration, and returns an MP4 plus editable source. A subsequent “make the labels bigger” reuses that task's artifacts. Sharing it with a teacher is a separate external action with recipient and attachment approval.
    
    General purpose means new workflows can compose the same capabilities and produce verifiable outputs. It does not mean every installed application or website works at launch.
    
    ## 4. Runtime architecture
    
    ```mermaid
    flowchart TD
      Phone[Phone or thin web client] --> API[Local backend: pairing, auth, task API]
      API --> Runtime[Me runtime adapter: Deep Agents and LangGraph]
      Runtime --> Model[Local model gateway]
      Runtime --> Memory[Authorized local memory service]
      Runtime --> Broker[Me tool broker and policy engine]
      Broker --> Approval[Persisted approval inbox]
      Approval --> API
      Broker --> Files[Scoped document and file tools]
      Broker --> Browser[Isolated browser worker]
      Broker --> Code[Isolated code and render workers]
      Broker --> Connectors[Approved service connectors and MCP]
      Browser --> Egress[Controlled external network access]
      Connectors --> Egress
      Runtime --> State[Local task state, checkpoints, events, artifacts]
    ```
    
    Deploy the backend, runtime, databases, inference, and worker infrastructure on Me Home. The `backend-server` name does not imply a cloud service. Runtime endpoints bind to loopback/internal networking; only the authenticated application API is exposed to paired clients over the local network.
    
    Use Python for the first runtime and worker integration because the shortlisted harness and browser/coding SDKs provide Python interfaces. Keep language-neutral JSON/OpenAPI contracts for clients. Use TypeScript inside animation workers where needed. This is a proposed stack, not an existing repository constraint.
    
    Use local PostgreSQL for application records and production checkpoints, plus an access-controlled local artifact directory. Use framework-compatible persistence adapters rather than inventing checkpoint serialization. Start with database full-text retrieval; add local embeddings/vector indexing only if retrieval evaluation justifies it. No hosted database, trace service, or vector store is required.
    
    ### Task lifecycle and recovery
    
    Public states: `queued`, `running`, `awaiting_approval`, `awaiting_input`, `succeeded`, `failed`, `cancelling`, `cancelled`. Track worker leases and recovery internally. A durable task ID is distinct from its conversation ID and framework checkpoint/thread ID.
    
    Persist the request and trusted identity, resolve allowed context, select tools, run a bounded think/tool/observe loop, check the result, and save artifacts plus a user-visible completion summary. Every step has a time, tool-call, output-size, and resource budget.
    
    After a process restart, recover expired worker leases and resume from persisted state. Reconstruct browser sessions where possible and revalidate page state before continuing. If an external action's outcome is unknown, enter reconciliation or ask the user; never blindly replay it.
    
    Framework checkpointing does not imply exactly-once external actions. Use stable action IDs, database transactions/outbox records, connector idempotency keys when supported, and confirmation reconciliation for other services. Nodes that resume after an interrupt may execute again; keep side effects outside replayable planning code.
    
    Stopping a task revokes future execution grants and terminates its workers. Already completed external actions may require a separate compensating action; the interface must report what happened.
    
    ## 5. Capabilities and execution environments
    
    ### Browser
    
    Use [browser-use](https://github.com/browser-use/browser-use) as the initial browser-agent candidate; it supports a local browser and local model configuration. Start with deterministic browser automation for known flows and use the agent for exploratory navigation. Confirm the selected release exposes interception points for every navigation and action; otherwise restrict it to an isolated read-only workflow or substitute a lower-level browser adapter.
    
    Give each user a dedicated browser profile and each task an isolated context where feasible. Scope account reuse explicitly; never share a parent's cookies with a child or import a system browser profile automatically. Provide interactive handoff for login, CAPTCHA, and MFA.
    
    The worker must enforce outbound destination rules, redirects, downloads, uploads, and access to local/private addresses. Test DNS rebinding and WebSocket/other browser egress, not only top-level URL strings. A home-network device requires an explicit separate connector grant.
    
    Prefer typed service APIs for sending, booking, or buying because their action payloads are easier to inspect and constrain. Browser commitments remain preview-and-confirm in the alpha. Site redesigns, anti-bot controls, and uncertain page state produce a handoff rather than invented success.
    
    ### Code and debugging
    
    Start with the chosen harness's brokered file/search/execute tools in a dedicated workspace. Implement the loop: inspect → edit → run a relevant test/command → read output → repair → verify. Bound iterations; return the actual failure when the budget expires.
    
    Workers receive only task files and explicitly imported source repositories. Mount inputs read-only where possible, keep generated outputs separate, run as an unprivileged user, cap CPU/memory/processes/storage, and deny network by default. Package installation uses a separately authorized dependency-fetch step or curated cached images.
    
    For household pilots, put untrusted execution behind a VM boundary; on a Linux appliance evaluate [gVisor](https://gvisor.dev/docs/) for compatible workers. Rootless containers can support the developer spike but are not the complete isolation argument. Never expose the host Docker socket, home directory, credential database, or unrestricted host terminal to the agent. Measure compatibility and overhead on the chosen hardware.
    
    Return diffs and test evidence. Publishing, pushing, opening a public endpoint, or deploying a created app requires its own grant. Add an [OpenHands SDK](https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk) worker only if it improves measured coding outcomes enough to justify another runtime; its internal terminal and file tools must obey the same environment and network boundaries.
    
    ### Animation and creative work
    
    Start with [Manim Community](https://github.com/ManimCommunity/manim), an MIT-licensed engine for programmatic explanatory animations. Add [Motion Canvas](https://github.com/motion-canvas/motion-canvas) for TypeScript-based informative motion graphics after the first renderer works. Both are rendering tools, not independent personal-agent frameworks.
    
    Use templates first: titles, diagrams, labels, transitions, charts, and simple scenes. Pipeline: brief → storyboard/scene specification → generated source → low-resolution render → inspect sampled frames and logs → bounded repair → final render → source/output artifact bundle. Reuse the coding worker's isolation rather than adding unrestricted render commands.
    
    Automated duration/codec/frame checks cannot establish that an animation teaches the right concept. Add rubric-based content and visual review; use a validated local vision model or human review for the alpha. Do not claim visual verification if no frame was actually inspected.
    
    Remotion can be a later adapter if its React authoring fits the product, but its [commercial-use terms](https://www.remotion.dev/docs/license) require a separate product decision. The current website's animated demo does not establish a reusable rendering backend. Generative image/video models are later optional capability packs with their own hardware and model-license requirements.
    
    ### Integrations and skills
    
    Provide typed first-party tools for memory, files, tasks, browser actions, execution, and artifacts. Add [MCP](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/learn/architecture) as an adapter for extensibility. Protocol compatibility is not permission enforcement: validate schemas, pin trusted servers, restrict their process/network access, and broker credentials.
    
    Each capability manifest declares its ID/version, input/output schemas, permissions, network destinations, filesystem roots, execution backend, resource budget, and completion checks. Skills provide instructions/examples/templates and reference those tools; they cannot grant themselves permissions.
    
    User-installed/community skills and automatically suggested improvements enter a reviewable, versioned state. Do not allow an agent to promote new executable code, dependencies, or broader grants simply because an earlier task succeeded. Run regression fixtures before enabling a changed skill.
    
    ## 6. Personalization, privacy, and household policy
    
    ### Memory design
    
    Separate conversation history/checkpoints, durable user preferences, user-approved household facts, retrieved documents, and artifacts. Every item carries household/user ownership, visibility, source, timestamps, retention, and deletion metadata.
    
    Perform authorization before retrieval and before constructing a model prompt. Include identity and visibility in cache keys and retrieval filters. A model prompt saying “do not reveal other users' data” is not an access-control system.
    
    Default private chats to the requesting user. Household sharing is explicit. Guardian control of a child's tools does not automatically imply access to every private conversation; define and disclose that product policy before a family pilot. Pairing and user switching must bind the active user to device credentials, not a user ID supplied in a prompt.
    
    Persist a preference from an explicit user instruction; ask about inferred or sensitive long-term memories. Show a memory viewer with correction, forget, export, and retention controls. Deletion must cover retrieval indexes, derived summaries, caches, and the relevant persisted conversation state; document backup expiry and what an exported artifact cannot retract.
    
    ### Permission enforcement
    
    The deterministic broker returns `allow`, `request_approval`, or `deny` for each action based on authenticated user, capability, exact operation, data scope, destination, and current household policy. The model may propose an action but cannot authorize it.
    
    | Action | Initial behavior |
    | --- | --- |
    | Read explicitly attached local files | Allow inside that task's scope |
    | Edit/run code in the isolated task workspace | Allow if the task granted that capability and budget |
    | Retrieve a different user's private memory | Deny |
    | Access external sites | Require a scoped external-access grant; show destinations and data involved |
    | Send, submit, upload, book, buy, or publish | Show exact commitment and request action approval |
    | Broad filesystem access, raw secrets, or host administration | Deny in the alpha |
    | Child request outside guardian policy | Deny or route to a guardian approval as the policy specifies |
    
    A user request such as “research these three sites” can provide scoped authorization when the interface clearly discloses external access. Avoid asking before every page read inside an existing grant. New destinations, private-data disclosures, accounts, and commitments require reevaluation.
    
    Approval records bind approver, task, action ID, canonical argument digest, destination, data/attachment references, policy version, expiration, and one-use status. The broker atomically claims the grant, rechecks current policy, and refuses changed arguments. Cross-device duplicate taps must not dispatch duplicate actions. Editing a proposed action creates a new approval. Delegated workers inherit a subset of the parent's grants.
    
    Browsers share IP addresses, request URLs, cookies, and potentially page-loaded third-party requests. The product must disclose that reality. “Only shopping-list items leave the house” is supportable only for a constrained connector with an inspected payload and a defined metadata disclosure, not arbitrary website browsing. Treat external content as untrusted data; never let a webpage, document, or tool result create a new grant.
    
    Store service credentials in a separate local secret broker, inject them only into authorized connectors, and redact logs. Keep application encryption keys separate from encrypted backups; define owner recovery and device-reset behavior. Use disk encryption and authenticated local transport. The local machine owner remains part of the trust boundary; row-level access control cannot protect against a malicious host administrator.
    
    ## 7. Models, hardware, and resource budgets
    
    Use one validated tool-calling local model first. [llama.cpp](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp) is a candidate inference server with quantization, multiple hardware backends, and an OpenAI-compatible API; [Ollama](https://github.com/ollama/ollama) is an alternative packaging/inference option. Choose one operational path for the alpha.
    
    Validate actual tool calling, argument schemas, stop behavior, streaming, cancellation, context truncation, image inputs where applicable, and structured output. An endpoint being OpenAI-compatible does not establish that the model follows the tools correctly. Review the selected weight license separately from the inference server license.
    
    Select model revisions through the fixture suite on an existing development machine, then validate on candidate appliance hardware before committing to a bill of materials. Compare a smaller and a larger local candidate at equal task budgets. Record RAM/VRAM including KV cache, throughput, time to first useful event, end-to-end task latency, idle/load power, and thermal behavior.
    
    Reserve interactive inference capacity while renders or code tasks run. Queue expensive work; expose progress and cancellation. Start with one heavy worker and increase concurrency only after measuring multi-user contention. Schedule model unload/load if necessary and report the latency penalty.
    
    Alpha defaults: local inference, local embeddings if enabled, local traces, disabled external telemetry, no cloud model fallback. Verify with network observation. Optional cloud inference would be a later, explicitly labeled mode requiring a product/privacy change; approval of a website action does not authorize uploading the entire chat to a model provider.
    
    ## 8. Repository and API boundaries
    
    | Repository | Responsibility |
    | --- | --- |
    | `agentic-framework` | Runtime adapter, capability contracts, broker/policy evaluation, checkpoints, memory access interfaces, workers, scheduler execution, artifacts, and agent evaluations |
    | `backend-server` | Paired-device identity, authentication, household/profile administration, public task/approval/artifact APIs, authenticated event delivery; invokes runtime using trusted identity |
    | `infra-server` | Local deployment, inference service operation, worker isolation, network policy, certificates/secrets provisioning, resource limits, updates/rollback, backup/restore |
    | `phone-app` | Pairing, chat/tasks, progress, approval inbox, artifact preview, memory/rule controls, notifications, and cancellation |
    | `web-app` | Existing public website/demo; optional separate authenticated development client, kept distinct from waitlist/signup |
    | `feed-algorithm` | Feed ranking and optimization; consumes authorized goals through a contract, without getting blanket chat-history access |
    
    The backend owns the client-facing API. The framework owns its internal typed commands/events and generates or publishes a versioned contract; do not expose framework checkpoint internals to phones. Backend auth establishes identity; runtime authorization independently enforces it. Policy administration and policy execution must share a versioned schema, not two separate rule implementations.
    
    Proposed application endpoints: create/list/get tasks, stream task events, cancel a task, list/resolve approvals, retrieve task artifacts, manage explicit memories, and create/disable schedules. Use idempotency keys on mutation requests, authenticated artifact authorization, pagination, and event replay cursors.
    
    Core records: `Task`, `Run`, `ToolAction`, `Approval`, `PolicyGrant`, `MemoryItem`, `Artifact`, `Schedule`, and versioned `TaskEvent`. Include actor, household, correlation IDs, schema versions, and timestamps. Persist event IDs so the client can reconnect without losing an approval or duplicating an outcome.
    
    User-visible events include task started, plan/progress summary, tool activity, approval requested/resolved, artifact ready, and task completed/failed/cancelled. Do not expose raw internal reasoning or unredacted tool logs as progress. Keep sensitive task metadata out of notification payloads.
    
    Suggested framework layout:
    
    ```text
    src/me_agent/
      contracts/       runtime/         models/
      policy/          approvals/       memory/
      tools/           capabilities/    workers/
      artifacts/       persistence/     scheduler/
    skills/            evals/           tests/
    docs/decisions/    examples/        pyproject.toml
    ```
    
    This layout is a proposal; bootstrap files remain intact until implementation begins.
    
    ## 9. Delivery sequence and ownership
    
    Planning assumption: three full-time engineers covering runtime/models, tools/isolation, and backend/client, with part-time product/design support. Target roughly 12 weeks to a constrained household alpha after kickoff; this is an estimate, not a consumer-launch commitment. Hardware, a new native client, or weak local-model results can extend it. A solo implementation should keep the same gates and substantially reduce scope.
    
    | Phase | Estimated window | Main deliverables | Exit gate |
    | --- | --- | --- | --- |
    | 0: choose foundation | Week 1 | Fixed fixtures, three-candidate experiment, model/hardware baseline, decision record | A documented local-only candidate passes mandatory policy controls and representative tasks |
    | 1: usable core | Weeks 2–3 | Runtime, local inference, persisted task/event API, thin client, pairing/auth, initial memory | An authenticated user submits a local task, reconnects, sees its result, and cannot access another user's task |
    | 2: safe execution | Weeks 4–5 | Broker, persisted approvals, per-user scopes, isolated code worker, artifacts, cancellation | Draft → approve → execute survives restart and rejects altered/replayed actions |
    | 3: capabilities | Weeks 6–8 | Browser research/draft workflows, code repair loop, Manim render loop, source/preview delivery | Research report, tested code patch, and checked animation all work through the client |
    | 4: personal agent | Weeks 9–10 | Editable memory, explicit household sharing, guardian policy, recurring schedules, resource queue | Two users keep private state isolated; a scheduled task respects current grants and can be disabled |
    | 5: household alpha | Weeks 11–12 | End-to-end regression suite, backup/restore, versioned deployment/rollback, onboarding, recovery drills | Release gates below pass on target hardware and a small consented pilot can operate without engineering intervention for normal tasks |
    
    Build the native phone shell in parallel once the task/event/approval contract stabilizes. A development web client can validate the runtime earlier; it does not make native phone delivery free. Remote access and public message channels remain later scope.
    
    ### Initial implementation backlog
    
    | ID | Work item | Owner | Depends on | Acceptance evidence |
    | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
    | AF-001 | Fixtures, candidate adapters, framework/model decision | Runtime | None | Reproducible report with versions, failures, resource measurements |
    | AF-002 | Task/event/action contracts and backend API skeleton | Runtime + backend | AF-001 | Generated client contract and reconnectable task fixture |
    | AF-003 | Paired-device authentication and user-scoped storage | Backend | AF-002 | Cross-user access tests, revocation, and reconnect flow |
    | AF-004 | Local model gateway and cancellation/budget support | Runtime | AF-001 | Real structured tool call, streamed response, timeout/cancel cases |
    | AF-005 | Persisted runtime/checkpoints and worker lease recovery | Runtime | AF-002, AF-004 | Kill/restart a run and complete without losing task identity |
    | AF-006 | Broker, grants, approval records, secret interface | Tools + backend | AF-003, AF-005 | Changed arguments, expired grants, and unauthorized identities rejected |
    | AF-007 | Isolated workspace executor and artifact store | Tools + infra | AF-006 | Host paths/secrets/egress unavailable; patch and test artifact returned |
    | AF-008 | Thin task/approval/artifact client | Client | AF-002, AF-003 | Submit → progress → approve/decline → inspect result → cancel |
    | AF-009 | Browser research and draft capability | Tools | AF-006, AF-007 | Local-browser fixtures, destination constraints, handoff and approval cases |
    | AF-010 | Animation capability and render verification | Tools | AF-007, AF-008 | Render, revise, export, and reopen editable source |
    | AF-011 | Durable memory and guardian policy integration | Runtime + backend | AF-003, AF-006 | Visibility, correction/deletion, and guardian decision fixtures |
    | AF-012 | Explicit schedules, update/restore drills, alpha release | Runtime + infra | AF-009–AF-011 | Schedule revocation, no duplicate commitments after restart, restored home state |
    
    First development slice after the selection: an authenticated user asks the local model to create a small file, receives a persisted artifact through the client, and can reconnect to the completed task. Add an approval-gated external action immediately afterward. This validates the integration backbone before broad capability work.
    
    ## 10. Evaluation and release gates
    
    Expand from the 30-task selection set to at least 60 versioned normal tasks before alpha, with held-out variants to detect tuning to templates. Maintain an independent adversarial suite. Prefer local deterministic websites and code fixtures for repeatability; label live-web results separately.
    
    Proposed alpha targets, to be confirmed after the first measurements:
    
    - At least 80% independently verified completion on the explicitly supported task suite, with at least 70% in every capability category. Report retries, intervention, unsupported cases, and repeat-run variance separately.
    - Zero observed unauthorized actions in tests for cross-user retrieval, approval mutation/replay, prompt-injection-driven scope expansion, secret access, and network/path escape. Passing tests is release evidence, not a guarantee that all attacks are solved.
    - Local chat/document/code/render workflows continue with WAN disconnected after initial dependency/model provisioning. External workflows report their dependency clearly.
    - No unapproved outbound data in observed network tests; inspect model, tool, telemetry, update, dependency-fetch, and browser paths separately.
    - Kill/restart tests before/after approval, before/after dispatch, after a remote service accepts an action, and during artifact writes. Uncertain outcomes reconcile without blind replay.
    - Cancellation prevents subsequent tool dispatch; targeted worker termination within a proposed five-second budget under normal conditions. Disclose operations already completed.
    - Baseline local chat targets p95 time to first useful output under five seconds on the declared hardware/model at one interactive user. Record cold-start and loaded-device results separately; revise supported hardware or models if missed.
    - Animation outputs meet declared duration/resolution and pass content/visual review; code changes pass task-relevant tests; research claims have inspectable sources. Agent self-report alone is not a completion judge.
    - Backup/restore and rollback work on a clean device; logs and notifications redact secrets; clients can export/delete authorized data.
    
    Operational metrics: completion by capability/model/version, approval frequency, refusal/block reasons, repairs per task, queue time, p50/p95 latency, peak RAM/VRAM/disk use, worker failures, and external destinations. Store diagnostics locally; sharing a diagnostic bundle is explicit and reviewable.
    
    ## 11. Deferred scope and decisions still needed
    
    After alpha: authenticated remote access, additional connectors/channels, stronger coding workers if justified, voice, richer rendering tools, desktop/computer use, proactive suggestions, and feed integration. Each reuses the same grants, artifacts, identity, and task lifecycle.
    
    Do not make the first milestone depend on a plugin marketplace, many simultaneous agents, model training, an autonomous self-modifying agent, or a universal computer-control layer. Purchases and similar real-world commitments remain preview-and-confirm until their connector-specific recovery is proven.
    
    Decisions that can proceed with defaults: Python runtime, embedded harness, local PostgreSQL, local inference, a thin client, Manim first, serial heavy workers, and local-network access only. These are reversible proposals.
    
    Decisions requiring evidence or product input: exact comparison-project URLs; target appliance hardware and budget; supported first-user workflows; whether guardian supervision includes any chat visibility; final model/weight license; existing team capacity; native-phone priority; and whether optional cloud inference should ever be offered. The evaluation, artifact pipeline, and core contracts can proceed before most of those choices are finalized.
    
    The recommended next milestone is the one-week framework/model experiment followed by a recorded decision. Implementation should then build one working end-to-end task path and expand capability by capability, with measurable correctness and privacy boundaries at every gate.

## Assistant

The plan is written. It separates the reusable agent engine from the controls Me must own, and includes a 12-week alpha estimate for three engineers, implementation tickets, API boundaries, and release gates.

Two constraints shape it: browser tasks need accurate disclosure of what leaves the home, and checkpointing alone cannot prevent duplicate external actions after a restart. The plan includes scoped network access and action reconciliation for those cases.

- Permissions governing every tool and external action.
- Persistent tasks, progress, approvals, cancellation, and recovery.
- Browser, coding, animation, and service integrations.
- Phone interaction and artifact previews.

The proposed capability stack is:

| Capability | Starting approach |
|---|---|
| General assistance | Deep Agents with a validated local tool-calling model |
| Browsing | Browser-use in isolated browser workers |
| Writing/debugging code | Scoped file and terminal tools; evaluate OpenHands if quality needs improvement |
| Animation | Manim first, then Motion Canvas |
| Additional integrations | Typed tools plus controlled MCP adapters |
| Personalization | Authorized local memory with inspect, edit, and forget controls |

These components have different roles: the agent decides and coordinates; browser/code/render workers execute; Me’s permission layer determines what they may access.

**The delivery plan targets a constrained household alpha in roughly 12 weeks**, assuming three full-time engineers and part-time product/design support:

| Window | Outcome |
|---|---|
| Week 1 | Compare frameworks and local models on the same tasks |
| Weeks 2–3 | Local agent, authentication, persistent tasks, thin client |
| Weeks 4–5 | Permissions, approvals, isolated execution, artifacts |
| Weeks 6–8 | Working browser, code/debug, and animation workflows |
| Weeks 9–10 | Personal memory, household rules, scheduled tasks |
| Weeks 11–12 | Recovery, backup/restore, hardware validation, alpha testing |

The document includes repository responsibilities, API/data contracts, twelve implementation tickets, acceptance tests, and release gates.

**The biggest uncertainty is local-model capability on the eventual home hardware.** Framework support for local models doesn’t establish that those models can reliably browse, debug, and repair generated animations. The first milestone measures that before we commit to the architecture or hardware.

4. Implementation roadmap
Phase 1 — Working autonomous agent

Deploy OpenMuse to our cloud infrastructure. Connect an AI model, persistent database, and E2B computer. Test research, browsing, files, and tasks that continue after the app closes.

Phase 2 — Intelligent task execution

Add dependency-aware planning, persistent project memory, independent subtasks, human clarification requests, and resumable workflows.

Phase 3 — Multi-user platform

Add user accounts, tenant isolation, cloud-computer lifecycle management, encrypted credentials, spending limits, and audit logs. Require approvals before consequential external actions.

Phase 4 — Product launch

Branded iOS app, push notifications, task dashboard, integrations, subscriptions or internal access management, and production monitoring.

The first technical milestone I'd target: Give the agent a research task, close the iPhone app, and confirm it can finish the research independently in its cloud computer, save the result, and send a notification. Then test whether it can ask for clarification while other subtasks continue.

That gives us a real autonomous agent foundation, not just a convincing chat interface.

One product assumption I'd make for now: we are building a platform that can eventually support multiple users, even though we start by testing with our own team. That means designing proper user isolation from the beginning rather than treating every user as a separate installation.

Sample mode stays on localhost and uses fictional data.\n# Every mode requires a server-only CopilotKit Intelligence project key.\nWORKSPACE_MODE=sample\nAGENT_BACKEND=sample\nPORT=8787\nHOST=127.0.0.1\nPUBLIC_API_URL=http://localhost:8787\nALLOWED_ORIGINS=http://localhost:8081,http://127.0.0.1:8081\nDATA_DIR=.openmuse\nTASK_WORKER_ENABLED=true\n# Rate limiting keys on the socket address. Set true only behind a reverse proxy that\n# overwrites X-Forwarded-For; otherwise callers can spoof it.\n# TRUST_PROXY=false\n\n# General delegated work: select AGENT_BACKEND=model and a provider/model.\n# MODEL=openai/your-model-id\n# OPENAI_API_KEY=\n# ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=\n# GOOGLE_API_KEY=\n# Keyless public web search is enabled by default. Queries and task/chat context go to Parallel.\n# Disable on the API and any separate task worker with WEB_SEARCH_ENABLED=false.\nWEB_SEARCH_ENABLED=true\n# Optional OpenAI-compatible Responses API endpoint:\n# OPENAI_BASE_URL=\n# Optional Anthropic endpoint override; a trailing /v1 is stripped (the SDK adds /v1 itself):\n# ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=\n# Optional Google AI endpoint override; a trailing /v1beta is stripped (the SDK adds /v1beta itself):\n# GOOGLE_GENERATIVE_AI_BASE_URL=\n# For a gateway model ID such as vendor/model, set MODEL=openai/vendor/model.\n# Providers whose /responses tool loop is incomplete (e.g. DeepSeek) can opt\n# into the Chat Completions wire format instead:\n# OPENAI_CHAT_COMPLETIONS=true\n\n# Live Google workspace: WORKSPACE_MODE=live, AGENT_BACKEND=model.\n# OPENMUSE_ACCESS_KEY=  # random secret, at least 24 characters\n# TOKEN_ENCRYPTION_KEY=  # 32 random bytes encoded as base64\n# GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID=\n# GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET=\n# OAuth callback is PUBLIC_API_URL + /api/google/callback\n\n# Optional separate task worker; all processes share DATA_DIR for PDF files.\n# DATABASE_URL=postgresql://...\n# Set TASK_WORKER_ENABLED=false on the API when using pnpm dev:worker.\n\n# Browser worker (separate from the task worker):\n# BROWSER_WORKER_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8790\n# WORKER_TOKEN=  # same random 32+ character secret in API and browser worker\nWORKER_DATA_DIR=.openmuse/browser-profiles\nWORKER_HOST=127.0.0.1\n\n# An optional external raw AG-UI agent replaces conversational routing only.\n# AGENT_BACKEND=agui\n# AGENT_URL=https://your-agent.example/run\n# AGENT_TOKEN=\n# OpenBot's Intelligence runtime is not this raw AG-UI URL. See its adapter docs.\n\n# CopilotKit Intelligence is required in every mode. Create or select a project\n# with the commands below, then keep the generated key server-only.\n# npx copilotkit@latest login\n# npx copilotkit@latest project select\nCPK_INTELLIGENCE_API_KEY=\n\n# CopilotKit SDK telemetry goes through the shared sink to PostHog, tagged OpenMuse.\n# project select also writes CPK_TELEMETRY_ID: preserve that generated value and\n# deploy it alongside CPK_INTELLIGENCE_API_KEY to link runtime usage to the account.\n# Do not invent an identity or copy one from another project.\n# CPK_TELEMETRY_ID=  # generated by the CLI; keep server-only\n# Full funnel capture is the default; an explicit sample rate overrides it.\n# COPILOTKIT_TELEMETRY_SAMPLE_RATE=1\n# Opt out of SDK telemetry with either flag (true or 1), then restart the API:\n# COPILOTKIT_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=true\n# DO_NOT_TRACK=1\n\n# Optional private Docker Linux computer (separate from the browser).\n# Build first: docker build -t openmuse-computer:local apps/computer\n# Docker must be reachable from the API and any separate task worker.\nCOMPUTER_ENABLED=false\nCOMPUTER_IMAGE=openmuse-computer:local\n# Optional deployment name shared by API and worker. When unset, a new install keeps a random\n# name in DATA_DIR; an install created before that keeps a hash of PUBLIC_API_URL.\n# COMPUTER_DEPLOYMENT_ID=  # e.g. from `openssl rand -hex 12`\n# Optional scoped Docker engine, e.g. DOCKER_CONTEXT=colima-openmuse\n# Or run each owner's computer in an E2B Desktop sandbox instead of Docker\n# (graphical desktop with internet access; see docs/COMPUTER.md):\n# COMPUTER_PROVIDER=e2b-desktop  # default: docker\n# E2B_API_KEY=  # server-only; required for e2b-desktop, never sent into the sandbox\n# COMPUTER_DEPLOYMENT_ID is required for e2b-desktop: sandboxes are matched across the E2B team\n# COMPUTER_E2B_TEMPLATE=desktop  # optional custom template built from \"desktop\"\n# E2B_DOMAIN=  # only when not using the default E2B cluster\n\n# Optional Jev interaction choices: off (default), sample scripted decisions, or live SDK.\nJEV_MODE=off\n# live sends the latest user message, agent-written context and candidate choices to TypeSafe;\n# see docs/demos/jev-generative-ui.md#what-live-mode-sends-to-typesafe\n# TYPESAFE_API_KEY=  # server-only; required for JEV_MODE=live\n# JEV_MODEL=jev-1.13.0\n","title":".env.example","modified_date":"2026-10-26T15:38:01Z","url":"https://github.com/CopilotKit/openmuse/blob/main/.env.example","display_url":"https://github.com/CopilotKit/openmuse/blob/main/.env.example","display_title":".env.example","structuredContent":{"title":".env.example","content":"# Copy to .env. See [what is verified](docs/VERIFICATION.md) and the [roadmap](ROADMAP.md).\n\n## Demo\n\nOn iPhone, ask OpenMuse to find interesting stories on Hacker News and summarize CopilotKit. On desktop, ask it to check the school-trip email, open the message, and research exhibits at Monterey Bay Aquarium. The agent shows email and browser results inline. **Take control** opens that same browser session when you need it.\n\nThe 38-second iPhone and 42-second desktop web demos show the current interface, framed in 16:9. The send arrow becomes a stop square inside the input pill while the agent replies, then switches back. Stopping keeps your draft intact. See the [recording notes](docs/DEMO.md) for the model setup and reproduction steps.\n\n[Mobile MP4](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/8014d185-346c-4954-8ff0-26c582c5093a) · [Web MP4](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/0cc87de0-c3c1-4f24-b7df-e7d04bb946fd) · [Recording details and reproduction](docs/DEMO.md)\n\nThe [Jev aquarium-trip demo](docs/demos/jev-generative-ui.md) walks through a fictional school email, clarification choices, sourced exhibit cards, hands-on preference refinement, and a confirmed selection. [Watch the 83-second live Jev recording](assets/demos/2026-09-23/jev-live-web.mp4), where TypeSafe Jev makes the decisions and a scripted agent keeps the trip scenario repeatable. A [scripted-decision sample recording](assets/demos/2026-09-23/jev-web.mp4) is also available.\n\n## What it is\n\nOpenMuse is a personal-agent application with an agent computer, visible work, and rich results. It runs its own server, task worker, and browser worker. You can inspect and change the source under the MIT license.\n\nThe computer combines **persistent Chromium and an optional Linux workspace**. The agent can browse public pages, run commands in its own container, work with files, and move PDFs between the computer and the app. You can open its browser or terminal and continue the work. Graphical desktops and autonomous checkout remain future work.\n\n## Features\n\n| Surface | What runs in this alpha |\n| --- | --- |\n| **Chat** | CopilotKit headless chat with streamed AG-UI events, mailbox search and reading, send/stop in one input pill, a visible follow-up queue, retained drafts, delegated tasks, and inline email, browser, PDF, plan, and finance cards. |\n| **Agent computer** | Persistent browser profiles and takeover console; optional isolated Linux terminal, saved command receipts, editable workspace files, and PDF transfer. |\n| **Activity** | Durable task plans, progress, input requests, pause/resume/cancel/retry, approvals, and saved receipts. SQL leases recover interrupted work. |\n| **Ideas** | Suggestions with source evidence; edit, accept, or dismiss. Sent replies and completed matching work are excluded. |\n| **Goals & Tracking** | Goals and milestones; recurring public-page checks for changes, text availability, or USD price thresholds, with deduplicated alerts and failure backoff. |\n| **Documents** | Email attachment → PDF → requested form values → filled copy → reviewed reply → receipt. Native/web PDF viewing, paging, zoom, supported fields, and sharing. |\n| **Finance** | Import transaction CSV to create a spending summary with categories, transactions, and a savings-goal action. |\n| **Gmail & Calendar** | Google OAuth adapters, complete mail threads, drafts/attachments, calendar discovery, and reviewed event creation/update/deletion. Live credentials required. |\n| **Personal context** | Editable name, tone, avatar, and memories. Background-update preferences and durable in-app notifications. |\n| **Rich Threads** | CopilotKit Intelligence persistence in every mode, with a stable main conversation, side chats, renaming, archiving, restoring, and replay. A server-only project key is required. |\n\nThe [feature inventory](docs/FEATURES.md) describes implemented capabilities and planned extensions. Health/bank/social connectors, device push, voice, generated executable tools, and automatic reservations/payments are on the [roadmap](ROADMAP.md).\n\n## Quick start\n\n**Requirements:** Node 24 LTS, pnpm 11.19.0, and a CopilotKit Intelligence project key. The local sample app needs no model, Google account, or Docker.\n\n```sh\ngit clone https://github.com/CopilotKit/OpenMuse.git openmuse\ncd openmuse\npnpm install --frozen-lockfile\ncp .env.example .env\nnpx copilotkit@latest login\nnpx copilotkit@latest project select\n# Set CPK_INTELLIGENCE_API_KEY in .env to the generated server-only project key.\n# Keep the CLI-generated CPK_TELEMETRY_ID too, including in deployed server environments.\npnpm dev\n```\n\nIn another terminal:\n\n```sh\npnpm dev:web\n```\n\nOpen [localhost:8081](http://localhost:8081). The API runs at [localhost:8787/api/health](http://localhost:8787/api/health).\n\n### Try it\n\n1. In Chat, send **“Complete the permission slip”**. Open the task, supply fictional form values, inspect the saved PDF, and review the prepared reply. This writes only to the local mailbox.\n2. In **Goals → Track**, create a built-in availability watch, then change the built-in test page to trigger an alert.\n3. In **Menu → Delegate task → Finance**, use **Try example transactions** to create an interactive spending tracker.\n4. Start the [browser worker](#browser-worker) and configure a model, then ask **“Check out Hacker News for cool stuff”** or **“Summarize copilotkit.ai”**. Follow the browser inline and use **Take control** to open its session. For a model-free version of this flow, follow the [AI Mock demo setup](docs/DEMO.md#run-the-agent-browser-demo).\n\nFor iOS or Android, use `pnpm --dir apps/mobile ios` or `pnpm --dir apps/mobile android`. Xcode or Android tooling is required. The PDF reader needs an Expo development build; use [native setup](apps/mobile/README.md).\n\n## Deploy on Render\n\n[![Deploy to Render](https://render.com/images/deploy-to-render-button.svg)](https://render.com/deploy?repo=https://github.com/CopilotKit/OpenMuse)\n\n[render.yaml](render.yaml) deploys three services: the API, the web app, and a private browser. The API answers `/` with JSON, so the UI is its own static site.\n\n### First run\n\n1. Click **Deploy to Render**. Wait until `openmuse-api`, `openmuse-web`, and `openmuse-browser` are live.\n2. On `openmuse-api`, open **Environment** and copy `OPENMUSE_ACCESS_KEY`.\n3. Open the `openmuse-web` URL and sign in with that key.\n4. Send a message.\n\nThe deploy form asks for three values you provide. Render generates the other two.\n\n| Variable | Set by | If it is missing |\n|---|---|---|\n| `CPK_INTELLIGENCE_API_KEY` | You. Run `npx copilotkit@latest login`, then `npx copilotkit@latest project select`. Keep it on the server. | Chat cannot open a thread. |\n| `CPK_TELEMETRY_ID` | You. Keep the identity generated by the same project selection. | Runtime usage cannot be attributed to the Intelligence signup account. |\n| `OPENAI_API_KEY` | You. Used by the default `openai/gpt-5`. Change `MODEL` and supply the matching provider key for Anthropic or Google. | The model call fails. |\n| `OPENMUSE_ACCESS_KEY` | Render | You cannot sign in. |\n| `TOKEN_ENCRYPTION_KEY` | Render | The API refuses to start in live mode. |\n\nHealth check: `https://<openmuse-api>/api/health`.\n\n### Services\n\n| Service | Plan | What it runs |\n|---|---|---|\n| `openmuse-api` | Standard, with a 1 GB disk at `/var/data` | The Hono API and the in-process task worker. `DATA_DIR` is `/var/data/openmuse`. |\n| `openmuse-web` | Static site | The Expo web export. `EXPO_PUBLIC_API_URL` is baked in at build time. |\n| `openmuse-browser` | Private service, Standard, 1 GB disk at `/data` | Playwright and Chromium. The API calls it on the private network. |\n\n**Standard** is the smallest plan that stays up. At 512 MB the process runs out of memory before it binds a port, because PGlite loads an embedded Postgres build.\n\n**The disk** holds the database, PDFs, and the signing key. A redeploy without it wipes that data. Chat threads are stored by CopilotKit Intelligence, so a thread can still load after you sign back in even when the disk was never attached.\n\n**Live mode** is required. Render binds `0.0.0.0`, and sample mode rejects any host that is not loopback. The Blueprint sets `WORKSPACE_MODE=live`.\n\n**Browsing is included, and you can take it out.** `openmuse-browser` is a private service, so it has no public URL. The API reaches it at `http://openmuse-browser:8790` with a token Render generates. If the private hostname is not `openmuse-browser`, set `BROWSER_WORKER_URL` to `http://<that-host>:8790`. To deploy without it, delete the `openmuse-browser` service and the `BROWSER_WORKER_URL` and `WORKER_TOKEN` entries on `openmuse-api`. Chat, drafts, and tasks still run. Page reads, screenshots, and **Take control** do not.\n\nThe Docker computer and Google mail or calendar need the setup in the sections below. This Blueprint does not start them.\n\n## Configure the agent and Google\n\nCopy the commented settings in [.env.example](.env.example) into your private `.env`:\n\n1. Set `AGENT_BACKEND=model`, `MODEL=provider/model-id`, and the matching provider key. CopilotKit supports the configured OpenAI, Anthropic or Google provider. Fictional data can still be used with a real model. Provider keys stay on the server.\n2. Create or select a CopilotKit Intelligence project with `npx copilotkit@latest login` and `npx copilotkit@latest project select`. Keep the generated `CPK_INTELLIGENCE_API_KEY` on the server.\n3. For personal mail/calendar, set `WORKSPACE_MODE=live`, the generated `CPK_INTELLIGENCE_API_KEY`, a random `OPENMUSE_ACCESS_KEY` of at least 24 characters, and `TOKEN_ENCRYPTION_KEY` containing 32 random bytes encoded as base64. Restart the API.\n4. Configure a Google OAuth web client with Gmail and Calendar APIs enabled. Set `GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID` and `GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET`; register `${PUBLIC_API_URL}/api/google/callback` as its redirect URI. Configure consent/test-user access in your Google project.\n5. Open **Apps → Gmail** (or **Google Calendar**), connect read access, and grant write access when needed. Every send or calendar change still requires its own stored review. Changing/disconnecting the account invalidates pending connection-bound work.\n\nGoogle credentials are encrypted at rest. File URLs and browser consoles use short-lived signatures. This deployment uses one owner protected by a shared access key; it is not a multi-tenant authentication system. Use HTTPS and restricted network access for a remote host. Keep the default local-data mode on loopback.\n\n## Public web search\n\nWeb search is enabled by default. Set `WEB_SEARCH_ENABLED=false` on the API and any separate task worker to disable it. With a configured model, delegated tasks and built-in model chat (`AGENT_BACKEND=model`) use [Parallel's free, keyless Search MCP](https://docs.parallel.ai/integrations/mcp/search-mcp) as their built-in search provider. Ask, for example, “Find the official CopilotKit React Native setup instructions and cite the sources.” Results include source URLs and excerpts; delegated tasks save them as evidence. Scripted sample chat and external AG-UI conversations keep their existing tools.\n\nSearch sends model-generated queries and context, which may include information from your conversation or task, plus a random per-chat/task session identifier to Parallel. See [Parallel's privacy policy](https://parallel.ai/privacy-policy). Free access is rate limited; failures are reported without a paid fallback. Stopping chat or interrupting a task cancels its search.\n\n## Browser worker\n\nSet `BROWSER_WORKER_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8790` and a random `WORKER_TOKEN` of at least 32 characters in `.env`.\n\n```sh\npnpm --dir apps/worker exec playwright install chromium\npnpm dev:browser\n```\n\nOr use `docker compose --env-file .env -f infra/compose.yaml up --build -d`. The same token must reach the API and worker. Sessions have persistent Chromium profiles; the app can open a live screenshot console and import PDF downloads. Agent tools can read public pages and hand interactive work to the person. [Worker setup and boundaries](apps/worker/README.md).\n\n## Persistence and operation\n\n### Linux terminal and workspace\n\nBuild the computer image, enable it on the API, then open **Computer → Terminal → Start computer**:\n\n```sh\ndocker build -t openmuse-computer:local apps/computer\nCOMPUTER_ENABLED=true pnpm dev\n```\n\nThe API needs access to the Docker CLI and engine. Commands run in a nonroot container with no host-directory mounts or credentials. A named `/workspace` volume retains files when stopped. Terminal networking is disabled; public web access uses the browser worker. Commands have a 30-second limit and saved output/exit receipts. **Files** supports folders, text editing, and PDF transfer to/from Documents. This is a Linux container, not a full operating-system VM. [Setup, Colima option, and boundaries](docs/COMPUTER.md).\n\n### Application storage\n\nBy default, embedded PGlite, documents and the signing key live in `.openmuse/`; browser profiles live in `.openmuse/browser-profiles/`. Keep that directory private and back it up. The API hosts the task worker. The host must remain running for background work.\n\nFor a separate task worker, configure the same `DATABASE_URL`, secrets and shared `DATA_DIR` for both processes, then set `TASK_WORKER_ENABLED=false` on the API and run `pnpm dev:worker`. PGlite cannot be opened by separate processes. Production commands are `pnpm build:server`, `pnpm start` and `pnpm start:worker`. Run one API instance; task workers coordinate through SQL leases.\n\nNo hidden retry occurs after an uncertain external write. Review its provider outcome before creating a replacement. Pausing/cancelling prevents subsequent task steps; an already approved in-flight provider request may finish.\n\n## CopilotKit Rich Threads\n\nEvery deployment requires `CPK_INTELLIGENCE_API_KEY` on the API server for CopilotKit Intelligence conversation persistence and replay. Create or select a project with `npx copilotkit@latest login` and `npx copilotkit@latest project select`, set the generated server-only key, and restart the API. The native menu uses `useThreads`; rich tool results link back to saved tasks, documents, and browser sessions.\n\nIntelligence is a separate service and is not included in this repository's MIT license. No project key is shipped. [Configuration and validation boundaries](docs/RICH-THREADS.md).\n\n## Signup and runtime tracking\n\nThe CopilotKit SDK sends runtime telemetry through the shared CopilotKit sink to PostHog with `accessibility_title: \"OpenMuse\"`. Telemetry defaults to full capture; explicit SDK opt-outs and sampling settings take precedence. Keep the CLI-generated `CPK_TELEMETRY_ID` alongside the server-only project key when deploying. Intelligence records completed account signups separately; OpenMuse runtime usage can be joined to those accounts after the sink resolves the identity. [Setup, opt-out and PostHog validation](docs/TELEMETRY.md).\n\n## Architecture\n\n```mermaid\nflowchart TD\n  Client[Expo / React Native / Web] -->|AG-UI and authenticated API| API[Hono + CopilotKit runtime]\n  API --> Tasks[Durable task worker]\n  API --> Threads[CopilotKit Intelligence required in every mode]\n  API --> Store[(PGlite or PostgreSQL)]\n  Tasks --> Store\n  Tasks --> Review[Stored action review]\n  Review --> Google[Gmail / Calendar adapters]\n  Tasks --> Browser[Chromium worker + persistent profiles]\n  API --> Browser\n  API --> Computer[Optional Docker Linux computer]\n  Tasks --> Computer\n  Computer --> Volume[(Persistent workspace volume)]\n  Tasks --> Files[PDF files + structured artifacts]\n  API -. future adapter .-> OpenBot[OpenBot]\n```\n\n| Directory | Purpose |\n| --- | --- |\n| `apps/mobile` | Shared iOS, Android, and web UI with CopilotKit headless hooks. |\n| `apps/server` | API, CopilotKit runtime, identity boundary, task engine, reviews, files, and persistence. |\n| `apps/worker` | Token-protected Playwright browser service with persistent profiles. |\n| `apps/computer` | Nonroot Linux image, bounded filesystem helper, and real container verification. |\n| `packages/domain` | Shared types and request validation. |\n| `packages/integrations` | Google and browser protocol adapters. |\n| `packages/backends` | Optional OpenBot HTTP adapter and its identity boundary. |\n| `tests` | Workflow, runtime, persistence, provider-contract, and authorization tests. |\n\n### OpenBot compatibility\n\nOpenMuse's native client and personal-agent workflows are independent of OpenBot. The disabled OpenBot adapter is pinned and contract-tested against upstream interfaces. Live user/session bridging, routine mapping, and computer backend wiring remain future work. OpenBot's Intelligence runtime is not a raw AG-UI endpoint. [Integration contract](docs/OPENBOT-INTEGRATION.md).\n\n## Development\n\n```sh\npnpm lint\npnpm typecheck\npnpm test\npnpm build:server\npnpm build:web\npnpm build:ios\npnpm build:android\npnpm --dir apps/worker typecheck\npnpm test:browser\npnpm test:computer\n```\n\nPlatform build scripts export JavaScript/Hermes bundles; they do not produce signed app binaries. Browser checks use controlled HTTP fixtures; the local check requires installed Chromium, and the container check requires Docker and registry access to build its image. CI also exercises the browser and Linux computer containers. See [contribution guidance](CONTRIBUTING.md) and [verification results](docs/VERIFICATION.md).\n\n## Contributing and license\n\nIssues and pull requests are welcome. Start with [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md), [ROADMAP.md](ROADMAP.md), and the [security policy](SECURITY.md).\n\nMIT licensed. Built by CopilotKit. Its original interface and fictional assets are included.
