    structured result: {"content":"# The agent computer\n\nOpenMuse combines a persistent browser with an optional Linux workspace for commands and files. The app and CopilotKit tools use the same authenticated computer service, so you can inspect what the agent ran and continue working with its results.\n\n## Start the Linux workspace\n\nThe API host needs Docker CLI access to a running Docker engine. Build the image from this repository:\n\n```sh\ndocker build -t openmuse-computer:local apps/computer\n```\n\nEnable it on the API and any separate task worker, then restart them:\n\n```dotenv\nCOMPUTER_ENABLED=true\nCOMPUTER_IMAGE=openmuse-computer:local\n```\n\nOpen **Computer → Terminal → Start computer**. Run `pwd` or `python3 --version`. Commands execute inside the Linux container with `/workspace` as their default working directory. Their output, exit code, and status appear in command history.\n\nIf Docker is unavailable, the app reports the connection error. There is no fallback that executes commands on the API host.\n\n### Optional isolated runtime on macOS\n\nColima is an open-source way to run Docker in a Linux VM. A separate profile keeps OpenMuse independent of other Docker workloads:\n\n```sh\nbrew install colima\ncolima start openmuse --cpus 2 --memory 3 --disk 12 --root-disk 12 \\\n  --vm-type vz --activate=false --mount none --ssh-config=false\nDOCKER_CONTEXT=colima-openmuse docker build -t openmuse-computer:local apps/computer\nDOCKER_CONTEXT=colima-openmuse COMPUTER_ENABLED=true pnpm dev\n```\n\nThe explicit context applies to that command and its child processes. It does not change the default Docker context. Stop this VM with `colima stop openmuse` when you no longer need it.\n\n### Run the computer on an E2B desktop (optional)\n\nInstead of Docker, each owner's computer can be an [E2B Desktop](https://e2b.dev/docs) sandbox: a Linux VM with an Xfce desktop, Firefox ESR, Google Chrome and LibreOffice. The API host needs no Docker engine, and you can watch and control the desktop from the app.\n\n```dotenv\nCOMPUTER_ENABLED=true\nCOMPUTER_PROVIDER=e2b-desktop\nE2B_API_KEY=e2b_...            # API and task worker only; never passed into the sandbox\nCOMPUTER_DEPLOYMENT_ID=...     # required and unique per install, e.g. `openssl rand -hex 12`\n# COMPUTER_E2B_TEMPLATE=desktop  # default; or a custom template built from it\n# E2B_DOMAIN=...                 # only for a non-default E2B cluster\n```\n\n`config.ts` never lets `.env` override a variable that is already set, so unset any `E2B_API_KEY`, `E2B_DOMAIN` or `E2B_API_URL` exported in your shell for another cluster before `pnpm dev`.\n\nOpen **Computer → Start computer**. A **Desktop** tab appears next to Browser, Terminal and Files while the computer runs. On web it embeds the live stream; on iOS and Android, **Open desktop** opens it in the system browser. The stream URL is returned only to the signed-in owner. Treat it as a bearer secret: anyone holding it gets full keyboard and mouse control until the next Stop. It carries a VNC password, and VNC authentication uses only its first 8 characters.\n\nHow it maps to the Docker contract:\n\n- **One sandbox per owner and deployment**, found by sandbox metadata across your whole E2B team. That is why `COMPUTER_DEPLOYMENT_ID` is required for this provider: two installs with the same id would share a sandbox. The app refuses to attach to a sandbox whose metadata, template or lifecycle it did not set.\n- **`/workspace` persists; processes do not.** Stop is a filesystem-only pause: every command and desktop app ends, and files are kept. After 15 idle minutes the sandbox pauses the same way. Commands and file operations count as activity; working inside the desktop does not. Opening the Desktop tab keeps the computer awake for 30 minutes, and the tab extends that every 2 minutes while it is visible, for up to an hour. A desktop opened in another browser tab or from the mobile app pauses about 30 minutes after the last refresh, so come back to the Desktop tab to extend it. Start resumes the sandbox and relaunches the desktop session. A paused sandbox is kept until you delete it; deleting it in the E2B dashboard deletes its `/workspace`.\n- **Commands** run as the template's `user` account (uid 1000) in `/workspace`, with the same 30-second limit, exit code 124 on timeout and 128 KB output cap. File operations reuse `apps/computer/files.py` over stdin.\n- **GUI apps from the terminal.** Commands run with `DISPLAY=:0`, so `firefox-esr https://copilotkit.ai >/dev/null 2>&1 &` opens on the desktop. Output is collected into temporary files, so a backgrounded app does not keep the command open, and it keeps running after the command returns. Discard a background app's output as shown: otherwise it keeps writing to a deleted temporary file for as long as it runs. A command whose output passes 32 MB is stopped.\n- **Command history is per provider.** Receipts from the Docker computer are not shown for the desktop, and the other way around.\n\n#### The agent sees and drives the desktop\n\nWith this provider the agent gets one more tool, `use_desktop`, in chat and in delegated tasks. It mirrors the shape of Anthropic's computer-use tool:\n\n| Action | Arguments | xdotool call |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| `screenshot` | none | none |\n| `left_click`, `double_click`, `right_click` | optional `coordinate` `[x, y]` | `mousemove --sync x y click 1` (`--repeat 2`, button 3) |\n| `mouse_move` | `coordinate` | `mousemove --sync x y` |\n| `type` | `text` (up to 1000 characters) | `type --delay 12 -- text` |\n| `key` | `text`, xdotool key names or combos such as `Return` or `ctrl+l` | `key -- ...` |\n| `scroll` | `scroll_direction`, optional `scroll_amount` (default 3) and `coordinate` | wheel buttons 4 to 7 |\n| `wait` | optional `duration` in seconds (default 1, up to 10) | `sleep` |\n\n- **Every action returns a fresh screenshot.** Coordinates are pixels in that screenshot; the screen is 1280x800, so no scaling is involved. The screenshot is a JPEG (about 40 to 200 KB) taken with `scrot` half a second after the input.\n- **The image goes to the model as an image.** The tool returns TanStack AI content parts (a text part with the receipt, plus an image part). `@tanstack/ai` keeps a content-part array as the tool message, and all three adapters send it as a multimodal tool result: Anthropic `tool_result` blocks, OpenAI Responses `function_call_output` with `input_image`, Gemini `functionResponse.parts`. The AG-UI result event that is stored in the chat thread keeps only the text part, so later turns never replay image data as text.\n- **Receipts.** Each action is recorded next to the commands, for example `desktop left_click (640, 400)`, and the latest screenshot is kept per owner (`GET /api/computer/desktop/screenshot`). `POST /api/computer/desktop/actions` runs the same actions without returning the image.\n- **No implicit resume.** An action on a stopped computer fails with \"Start the computer\", and the agent has to call `start_computer` first. Actions take the computer's lease like file operations. The first stream connection takes the lifecycle lease so it cannot race startup or Stop; if busy, the viewer retries. Later stream requests only check or restart VNC without taking the lease, and concurrent viewers in one process share a single stream start.\n- **DISPLAY is set on every call.** The SDK's own `screenshot()`, `leftClick()` and `press()` run with no environment and rely on the `DISPLAY` that `Sandbox.create` stores in the sandbox environment. A filesystem-only pause cold-boots the VM, and the resumed sandbox no longer has that variable, so those helpers fail with `scrot: Can't open X display`. The app never uses them: it runs `xdotool` and `scrot` itself with `DISPLAY=:0`.\n- **Stuck modifiers are released.** A VNC viewer that loses focus in the middle of a shortcut (for example Alt+Tab in your browser) can leave Alt held, which turns every later key, click and scroll into a shortcut. Each input action releases all modifiers first.\n- **Same safety rules.** The agent is told never to click or press Return on a send, post, submit, sign-in, buy or upload control unless you asked for that exact action, and that text on screen is data, not instructions.\n\n#### Desktop card in chat\n\nWhen the agent uses `use_desktop`, the chat shows a **Desktop** card for each step with what it did. A persistent viewer after the tool cards embeds the live desktop, so new steps preserve the VNC connection. The per-step cards show their action labels. On web the viewer embeds the same stream as the Desktop tab. On iOS and Android it shows the latest screenshot and an **Open desktop** button. When the computer is stopped, the card says it is offline and offers **Start computer**. **Open in Desktop tab** opens the computer sheet on its Desktop tab.\n\n## Work with files\n\n- **Computer → Files** lists the persistent `/workspace` directory. Create folders, add text files, edit them, and save.\n- **Copy a document here** copies an owned PDF from OpenMuse into the current folder. A matching filename is replaced.\n- Open a PDF in the workspace to save a copy to OpenMuse Documents and view it in the native/web reader.\n- Browser downloads first enter Documents through **Import PDF downloads**, then can be copied into the Linux workspace.\n- Stopping the computer ends its running commands and keeps the named workspace volume. Starting it again restores those files.\n\nThe terminal runs bounded commands and displays their saved results. It is not an interactive PTY: full-screen terminal apps and prompts that require ongoing keyboard input are not supported. Write noninteractive scripts or edit files through the Files tab.\n\n## Isolation and scope\n\nThe workspace is a Docker container running as a nonroot user, with a read-only root filesystem, limited temporary storage and resources, dropped capabilities, and no added privileges. It receives no host directory mounts, Docker socket, model keys, Google tokens, or API access key. A named volume provides persistent `/workspace` storage.\n\nTerminal networking is disabled. The existing browser worker handles public web access through its own destination checks; see its [network boundary](../apps/worker/README.md#network-boundary). Browser profiles and workspace files have separate storage and lifecycle controls.\n\nThe E2B desktop provider differs from Docker in these ways:\n\n- **Network access is on.** The desktop's browsers need it, so commands can reach the internet too, and the app reports `network: enabled`. Treat anything downloaded as untrusted. This is also an outbound path the app does not review: the agent could post a file from `/workspace` or submit a form in Firefox, and only the app's own tools (`prepare_email`, `prepare_event`) require approval. The agent is told never to send, post or submit from the computer without an explicit request; that is an instruction, not an enforced boundary.\n- **Isolation comes from the VM.** Each owner gets a dedicated VM instead of a container on a shared kernel. Inside it there is no read-only root filesystem, capability drop or pids limit, and the template's `user` account has passwordless sudo.\n- **Every listening port is public.** Public traffic is enabled for the direct desktop iframe. Any service listening in the VM is reachable without app authentication at `https://<port>-<sandboxId>.e2b.app`; the sandbox ID is visible in the stream URL. Running `python3 -m http.server 8000` from `/workspace` exposes workspace files. Do not leave servers running, and stop temporary services as soon as they are no longer needed. The VNC password protects VNC only, not other services.\n- **Files live with E2B.** Workspace files are stored with E2B, outside your host. Your E2B plan's runtime limits apply.\n\nThe E2B API key stays on the API host.\n\nThis is a self-hosted, single-owner computer environment. Docker isolation does not provide a dedicated operating-system VM or a hostile-tenant security guarantee. The optional Colima VM provides the Linux host on macOS; the application still manages a Docker container within it.\n","title":"COMPUTER.md","modified_date":"2026-10-02T21:50:26Z","url":"https://github.com/CopilotKit/openmuse/blob/a4944f4c471d3dc93b8bfc060b5da309b5216ab2/docs/COMPUTER.md","display_url":"https://github.com/CopilotKit/openmuse/blob/a4944f4c471d3dc93b8bfc060b5da309b5216ab2/docs/COMPUTER.md","display_title":"COMPUTER.md","structuredContent":{"title":"COMPUTER.md","content":"# The agent computer\n\nOpenMuse combines a persistent browser with an optional Linux workspace for commands and files. It mirrors the shape of Anthropic's computer-use tool:\n\n| Action | Arguments | xdotool call |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| `screenshot` | none | none |\n| `left_click`, `double_click`, `right_click` | optional `coordinate` `[x, y]` | `mousemove --sync x y click 1` (`--repeat 2`, button 3) |\n| `mouse_move` | `coordinate` | `mousemove --sync x y` |\n| `type` | `text` (up to 1000 characters) | `type --delay 12 -- text` |\n| `key` | `text`, xdotool key names or combos such as `Return` or `ctrl+l` | `key -- ...` |\n| `scroll` | `scroll_direction`, optional `scroll_amount` (default 3) and `coordinate` | wheel buttons 4 to 7 |\n| `wait` | optional `duration` in seconds (default 1, up to 10) | `sleep` |\n\n- **Every action returns a fresh screenshot.** Coordinates are pixels in that screenshot; the screen is 1280x800, so no scaling is involved. The screenshot is a JPEG (about 40 to 200 KB) taken with `scrot` half a second after the input.\n- **The image goes to the model as an image.** The tool returns TanStack AI content parts (a text part with the receipt, plus an image part). `@tanstack/ai` keeps a content-part array as the tool message, and all three adapters send it as a multimodal tool result: Anthropic `tool_result` blocks, OpenAI Responses `function_call_output` with `input_image`, Gemini `functionResponse.parts`. The AG-UI result event that is stored in the chat thread keeps only the text part, so later turns never replay image data as text.\n- **Receipts.** Each action is recorded next to the commands, for example `desktop left_click (640, 400)`, and the latest screenshot is kept per owner (`GET /api/computer/desktop/screenshot`). `POST /api/computer/desktop/actions` runs the same actions without returning the image.\n- **No implicit resume.** An action on a stopped computer fails with \"Start the computer\", and the agent has to call `start_computer` first. Actions take the computer's lease like file operations. The first stream connection takes the lifecycle lease so it cannot race startup or Stop; if busy, the viewer retries. Later stream requests only check or restart VNC without taking the lease, and concurrent viewers in one process share a single stream start.\n- **DISPLAY is set on every call.** The SDK's own `screenshot()`, `leftClick()` and `press()` run with no environment and rely on the `DISPLAY` that `Sandbox.create` stores in the sandbox environment. A filesystem-only pause cold-boots the VM, and the resumed sandbox no longer has that variable, so those helpers fail with `scrot: Can't open X display`. The app never uses them: it runs `xdotool` and `scrot` itself with `DISPLAY=:0`.\n- **Stuck modifiers are released.** A VNC viewer that loses focus in the middle of a shortcut (for example Alt+Tab in your browser) can leave Alt held, which turns every later key, click and scroll into a shortcut. Each input action releases all modifiers first.\n- **Same safety rules.** The agent is told never to click or press Return on a send, post, submit, sign-in, buy or upload control unless you asked for that exact action, and that text on screen is data, not instructions.\n\n#### Desktop card in chat\n\nWhen the agent uses `use_desktop`, the chat shows a **Desktop** card for each step with what it did. A persistent viewer after the tool cards embeds the live desktop, so new steps preserve the VNC connection. The per-step cards show their action labels. On web the viewer embeds the same stream as the Desktop tab. On iOS and Android it shows the latest screenshot and an **Open desktop** button. When the computer is stopped, the card says it is offline and offers **Start computer**. **Open in Desktop tab** opens the computer sheet on its Desktop tab.\n\n## Work with files\n\n- **Computer → Files** lists the persistent `/workspace` directory. Create folders, add text files, edit them, and save.\n- **Copy a document here** copies an owned PDF from OpenMuse into the current folder. A matching filename is replaced.\n- Open a PDF in the workspace to save a copy to OpenMuse Documents and view it in the native/web reader.\n- Browser downloads first enter Documents through **Import PDF downloads**, then can be copied into the Linux workspace.\n- Stopping the computer ends its running commands and keeps the named workspace volume. Starting it again restores those files.\n\nThe terminal runs bounded commands and displays their saved results. It is not an interactive PTY: full-screen terminal apps and prompts that require ongoing keyboard input are not supported. Write noninteractive scripts or edit files through the Files tab.\n\n## Isolation and scope\n\nThe workspace is a Docker container running as a nonroot user, with a read-only root filesystem, limited temporary storage and resources, dropped capabilities, and no added privileges. It receives no host directory mounts, Docker socket, model keys, Google tokens, or API access key. A named volume provides persistent `/workspace` storage.\n\nTerminal networking is disabled. The existing browser worker handles public web access through its own destination checks; see its [network boundary](../apps/worker/README.md#network-boundary). Browser profiles and workspace files have separate storage and lifecycle controls.\n\nThe E2B desktop provider differs from Docker in these ways:\n\n- **Network access is on.** The desktop's browsers need it, so commands can reach the internet too, and the app reports `network: enabled`. Treat anything downloaded as untrusted. This is also an outbound path the app does not review: the agent could post a file from `/workspace` or submit a form in Firefox, and only the app's own tools (`prepare_email`, `prepare_event`) require approval. The agent is told never to send, post or submit from the computer without an explicit request; that is an instruction, not an enforced boundary.\n- **Isolation comes from the VM.** Each owner gets a dedicated VM instead of a container on a shared kernel. Inside it there is no read-only root filesystem, capability drop or pids limit, and the template's `user` account has passwordless sudo.\n- **Every listening port is public.** Public traffic is enabled for the direct desktop iframe. Any service listening in the VM is reachable without app authentication at `https://<port>-<sandboxId>.e2b.app`; the sandbox ID is visible in the stream URL. Running `python3 -m http.server 8000` from `/workspace` exposes workspace files. Do not leave servers running, and stop temporary services as soon as they are no longer needed. The VNC password protects VNC only, not other services.\n- **Files live with E2B.** Workspace files are stored with E2B, outside your host. Your E2B plan's runtime limits apply.\n\nThe E2B API key stays on the API host.\n\nThis is a self-hosted, single-owner computer environment. Docker isolation does not provide a dedicated operating-system VM or a hostile-tenant security guarantee. The optional Colima VM provides the Linux host on macOS; the application still manages a Docker container within it.\n","display_url":"https://github.com/CopilotKit/openmuse/blob/a4944f4c471d3dc93b8bfc060b5da309b5216ab2/docs/COMPUTER.md"}}

## Assistant

OpenMuse does have an E2B desktop adapter, which makes it worth prototyping. Its current limits matter, though: it uses a single-owner login, requires CopilotKit Intelligence for chat persistence, and its E2B desktop allows outbound traffic that can bypass approval checks. The chat follow-up queue also lives in the open app.

I’ll revise the plan to reuse its interface and existing task machinery while making durable task dependencies, tenant isolation, and enforceable tool permissions explicit work items.

Each provider SDK retries transient failures up to MODEL_MAX_RETRIES times.\nfunction adapter(spec: string) {\n  const [, provider = \"\", model = \"\"] = spec.trim().match(/^([^/:]*)[/:](.*)$/) ?? [];\n  if (!provider || !model.trim())\n    throw new Error(\n      `Invalid model string \"${spec}\". Use \"openai/gpt-5\", \"anthropic/claude-sonnet-4.5\", or \"google/gemini-2.5-pro\".`,\n    );\n  const id = model.trim();\n  switch (provider.toLowerCase()) {\n    case \"openai\":\n      // OpenAI-compatible endpoints that do not implement the Responses API\n      // tool loop (e.g. DeepSeek) can opt into the Chat Completions wire format.\n      if (process.env.OPENAI_CHAT_COMPLETIONS === \"true\")\n        return openaiChatCompletions(id as OpenAIChatModel, {\n          baseURL: process.env.OPENAI_BASE_URL,\n          maxRetries: MODEL_MAX_RETRIES,\n        });\n      return openaiText(id as OpenAIChatModel, {\n        baseURL: process.env.OPENAI_BASE_URL,\n        maxRetries: MODEL_MAX_RETRIES,\n      });\n    case \"anthropic\":\n      // The AI SDK base URL ends in /v1; the Anthropic SDK adds /v1 itself.\n      return anthropicText(id as AnthropicChatModel, {\n        baseURL: process.env.ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL?.replace(/\\/v1\\/?$/, \"\"),\n        maxRetries: MODEL_MAX_RETRIES,\n      });\n    case \"google\":\n    case \"gemini\":\n    case \"google-gemini\":\n      // The AI SDK base URL ends in /v1beta; @google/genai adds the API version itself.\n      return geminiText(id as GeminiTextModel, {\n        httpOptions: {\n          baseUrl: process.env.GOOGLE_GENERATIVE_AI_BASE_URL?.replace(/\\/v1beta\\/?$/, \"\"),\n          // @google/genai counts the first call in `attempts`.\n          retryOptions: { attempts: MODEL_MAX_RETRIES + 1 },\n        },\n      });\n    default:\n      throw unknownProvider(provider, spec);\n  }\n}\n\n/** With OPENAI_BASE_URL set, a gateway model ID most likely needs the openai/ prefix. */\nexport function unknownProvider(\n  provider: string,\n  spec: string,\n  baseUrl = process.env.OPENAI_BASE_URL,\n) {\n  const hint = baseUrl?.trim()\n    ? ` For a model on your OPENAI_BASE_URL gateway, use \"openai/${spec.trim()}\".`\n    : \"\";\n  return new Error(\n    `Unknown provider \"${provider}\" in \"${spec}\". Supported: openai, anthropic, google (gemini).${hint}`,\n  );\n}\n\n// The classic BuiltInAgent always offers these two state tools. The converter turns their\n// results into STATE_SNAPSHOT / STATE_DELTA events.\nconst stateTools = [\n  defineTool({\n    name: \"AGUISendStateSnapshot\",\n    description: \"Replace the entire application state with a new snapshot\",\n    parameters: z.object({ snapshot: z.any().describe(\"The complete new state object\") }),\n    execute: async ({ snapshot }) => ({ success: true, snapshot }),\n  }),\n  defineTool({\n    name: \"AGUISendStateDelta\",\n    description: \"Apply incremental updates to application state using JSON Patch operations\",\n    parameters: z.object({\n      delta: z\n        .array(\n          z.object({\n            op: z.enum([\"add\", \"replace\", \"remove\"]).describe(\"The operation to perform\"),\n            path: z.string().describe(\"JSON Pointer path (e.g., '/foo/bar')\"),\n            value: z\n              .any()\n              .optional()\n              .describe(\n                \"The value to set. Required for 'add' and 'replace' operations, ignored for 'remove'.\",\n              ),\n          }),\n        )\n        .describe(\"Array of JSON Patch operations\"),\n    }),\n    execute: async ({ delta }) => ({ success: true, delta }),\n  }),\n];\n\n/** A BuiltInAgent in TanStack factory mode with the options of the classic AI SDK mode. */\nexport function tanstackAgent(options: {\n  model: string;\n  maxSteps: number;\n  tools: ToolDefinition[];\n  prompt: string;\n  /** Checked between model turns, after the current turn's tools have settled. */\n  shouldContinue?: () => boolean;\n  /** Said when the step limit, not the model, ends a run; otherwise the reply just stops. */\n  stepLimitNote?: string;\n}) {\n  const agent = new BuiltInAgent({\n    type: \"tanstack\",\n    factory: ({ input, abortController }) => {\n      const converted = convertInputToTanStackAI(input);\n      // Build the system prompt like the classic mode. It does not forward system messages.\n      let system = options.prompt;\n      if (input.context.length) {\n        system += \"\\n## Context from the application\\n\";\n        for (const ctx of input.context) system += `${ctx.description}:\\n${ctx.value}\\n`;\n      }\n      if (\n        input.state !== undefined &&\n        input.state !== null &&\n        !(typeof input.state === \"object\" && Object.keys(input.state).length === 0)\n      )\n        system += `\\n## Application State\\nThis is state from the application that you can edit by calling AGUISendStateSnapshot or AGUISendStateDelta.\\n\\`\\`\\`json\\n${JSON.stringify(input.state, null, 2)}\\n\\`\\`\\`\\n`;\n      return chat({\n        adapter: adapter(options.model),\n        messages: converted.messages,\n        systemPrompts: system ? [system] : [],\n        tools: [\n          ...converted.tools,\n          ...[...options.tools, ...stateTools].map((tool) =>\n            toolDefinition({\n              name: tool.name,\n              description: tool.description,\n              inputSchema: tool.parameters as SchemaInput,\n            }).server((args) => (tool.execute as (args: unknown) => Promise<unknown>)(args)),\n          ),\n        ],\n        agentLoopStrategy: (state) =>\n          maxIterations(options.maxSteps)(state) && (options.shouldContinue?.() ?? true),\n        abortController,\n      });\n    },\n  });\n  const run = agent.run.bind(agent);\n  agent.run = (input: RunAgentInput) => {\n    const events = splitTextAtToolCalls(run(input)).pipe(map(textOnlyToolResult));\n    return options.stepLimitNote\n      ? reportStepLimit(events, options.maxSteps, options.stepLimitNote)\n      : events;\n  };\n  return agent;\n}\n\n/**\n * A tool can return TanStack content parts, e.g. text plus a screenshot. Keep only the text parts there.\n */\nexport function textOnlyToolResult(event: BaseEvent): BaseEvent {\n  if (event.type !== EventType.TOOL_CALL_RESULT) return event;\n  const content = (event as { content?: unknown }).content;\n  if (typeof content !== \"string\" || !content.startsWith(\"[\")) return event;\n  let parts: unknown;\n  try {\n    parts = JSON.parse(content);\n  } catch {\n    return event;\n  }\n  if (!isContentPartArray(parts)) return event;\n  const text = parts.flatMap((part) => (part.type === \"text\" ? [part.content] : []));\n  return { ...event, content: text.join(\"\\n\") } as BaseEvent;\n}\n\n/**\n * maxIterations ends the loop after the last allowed tool step without a final model reply.\n * When a run ends that way, add a short assistant message so it does not stop silently.\n */\nexport function reportStepLimit(events: Observable<BaseEvent>, maxSteps: number, note: string) {\n  let steps = 0;\n  let phase: \"text\" | \"calling\" | \"results\" = \"text\";\n  return events.pipe(\n    mergeMap((event): BaseEvent[] => {\n      if (event.type === EventType.TOOL_CALL_START) {\n        // Parallel calls of one model step arrive together; results end the step.\n        if (phase !== \"calling\") steps++;\n        phase = \"calling\";\n      } else if (event.type === EventType.TOOL_CALL_RESULT) phase = \"results\";\n      else if (event.type === EventType.TEXT_MESSAGE_CHUNK) phase = \"text\";\n      else if (event.type === EventType.RUN_FINISHED && phase === \"results\" && steps >= maxSteps)\n        return [\n          {\n            type: EventType.TEXT_MESSAGE_CHUNK,\n            messageId: randomUUID(),\n            role: \"assistant\",\n            delta: note,\n          } as BaseEvent,\n          event,\n        ];\n      return [event];\n    }),\n  );\n}\n\n// ponytail: the TanStack converter in @copilotkit/runtime 1.70.1 uses one message ID for the\n// whole run. Remove this when it starts a new ID for each step, like the classic mode does.\n// Text after a tool call gets a new message ID, so each step's text is a separate message.\nfunction splitTextAtToolCalls(events: Observable<BaseEvent>) {\n  let messageId: string | undefined;\n  let afterToolCall = false;\n  return events.pipe(\n    map((event) => {\n      if (event.type === EventType.TEXT_MESSAGE_CHUNK) {\n        if (!messageId || afterToolCall) messageId = randomUUID();\n        afterToolCall = false;\n        return { ...event, messageId };\n      }\n      if (event.type === EventType.TOOL_CALL_START) {\n        afterToolCall = true;\n        return messageId ? { ...event, parentMessageId: messageId } : event;\n      }\n      if (event.type === EventType.TOOL_CALL_RESULT) afterToolCall = true;\n      return event;\n    }),\n  );\n}\n","display_url":"https://github.com/CopilotKit/openmuse/blob/a4944f4c471d3dc93b8bfc060b5da309b5216ab2/apps/server/src/engine/tanstack-agent.ts"}}

    # Me: independent cloud personal-agent plan
    
    Status: proposed plan, superseding the home-local plan for the current phase. Research and source inspection: 2026-11-02. No cloud resources have been provisioned and no upstream runtime has been executed in this workspace.
    
    ## 1. Confirmed direction
    
    Build a general-purpose personal agent for our own team first, with a path to multiple independent users. Each user directs an agent through iOS/web; the agent uses our remote infrastructure and its own computer. It must continue after the client closes, preserve work, ask questions while independent work progresses, and return usable deliverables.
    
    Core workflows: research, public-web browsing, document/file work, writing and debugging code, and creating animations. Connected-account actions follow after the execution and approval boundaries are proven. Persistent memory and explicit scheduled work make this a personal agent across sessions.
    
    The existing Me website describes private inference and storage at home. This cloud phase changes that deployment and data boundary. Before exposing the prototype to users, clearly label where chat, memory, files, browser state, and model requests go. Do not carry the website's home-local claims into the cloud product. A later home-hosted executor can implement the same contracts; it is not a prerequisite for this prototype.
    
    ## 2. Recommended starting point
    
    **Prototype from a pinned OpenMuse revision, retain its TypeScript/Expo stack and existing SQL-backed worker, and build Me's durable task graph and execution policy around it.** Treat OpenMuse as a reusable application starter, rather than assuming it is already a complete multi-user autonomous platform.
    
    Source inspected: [CopilotKit/openmuse at a4944f4c471d3dc93b8bfc060b5da309b5216ab2](https://github.com/CopilotKit/openmuse/tree/a4944f4c471d3dc93b8bfc060b5da309b5216ab2). The repository is MIT-licensed. Its interface, browser service, task views, artifact flows, and review machinery offer a concrete reuse path. This is a source-based assessment; product quality still needs a live experiment.
    
    Do not start by combining OpenMuse, FastAPI, Deep Agents, OpenAI Agents SDK, LangGraph, and Temporal. They overlap in runtime and task responsibilities. First prove the existing path. Keep a harness adapter boundary so a later agent-engine replacement does not rewrite the task API or client.
    
    The proprietary products named in the discussion establish desired behavior, not verified information about their internal architectures. This plan does not depend on claims about their launch dates or implementation stacks.
    
    ### What source inspection actually establishes
    
    | Area | Observed upstream implementation | Consequence for Me |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | Client and API | Expo/React Native/web with Hono, CopilotKit, and AG-UI; built-in model path uses TanStack AI | Reuse TypeScript initially; a Python API rewrite has no demonstrated benefit |
    | Persistent work | SQL task leases, checkpoints, progress, approval waits, and multiple eligible tasks in the worker | Extend this engine first; explicitly test subtask dependency semantics |
    | Follow-up queue | Chat follow-ups are retained by the open app; delegated tasks run server-side | Move task-related questions/answers and follow-ups to a durable server inbox |
    | Identity | Shared-key login resolves the current workspace to a single owner | Replace with real account identity before multiple people share a deployment |
    | Computer | Optional E2B Desktop provider exists alongside Docker execution | We can prototype remote execution without building a desktop host from scratch |
    | Threads | CopilotKit Intelligence is required in all current modes | Decide whether to accept that service or replace thread persistence; self-hosting this repo does not remove that dependency |
    | Verification | Upstream records fixture and browser/container tests, with live-model and account tests remaining separate | Run our own acceptance suite; upstream recordings do not establish open-ended autonomous quality |
    
    Evidence: [runtime](https://github.com/CopilotKit/openmuse/blob/a4944f4c471d3dc93b8bfc060b5da309b5216ab2/apps/server/src/agent.ts), [worker](https://github.com/CopilotKit/openmuse/blob/a4944f4c471d3dc93b8bfc060b5da309b5216ab2/apps/server/src/engine/worker.ts), [authentication](https://github.com/CopilotKit/openmuse/blob/a4944f4c471d3dc93b8bfc060b5da309b5216ab2/apps/server/src/auth.ts), [threads](https://github.com/CopilotKit/openmuse/blob/a4944f4c471d3dc93b8bfc060b5da309b5216ab2/docs/RICH-THREADS.md), and [verification boundaries](https://github.com/CopilotKit/openmuse/blob/a4944f4c471d3dc93b8bfc060b5da309b5216ab2/docs/VERIFICATION.md). The verification document predates some current source changes; its test counts are not a report of tests run on our selected revision.
    
    ## 3. Architecture and component choices
    
    ```mermaid
    flowchart TD
      Client[Expo iOS and web client] --> API[Authenticated Me API]
      API --> State[PostgreSQL: tasks, steps, questions, approvals, events]
      API --> Inbox[Durable follow-up inbox]
      State --> Scheduler[Dependency scheduler and leased workers]
      Inbox --> Scheduler
      Scheduler --> Harness[Agent harness adapter]
      Harness --> Models[Configurable model provider]
      Harness --> Memory[User and project scoped memory]
      Harness --> Policy[Tool broker: identity, grants, budgets]
      Policy --> Computer[E2B remote execution adapter]
      Policy --> Browser[Controlled browser service]
      Policy --> Connectors[Typed integrations and approved MCP tools]
      Computer --> Objects[Artifact object storage]
      Scheduler --> Events[Persisted progress and notification outbox]
      Events --> Client
      Events --> Push[APNs or Expo notification delivery]
    ```
    
    | Component | First implementation | Replacement condition |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | Mobile/web | Reuse OpenMuse Expo/React Native components and AG-UI presentation | Replace specific screens when Me's workflows require it |
    | API and agent | Reuse Hono/TypeScript and current built-in agent behind an adapter | Evaluate Deep Agents if measured planning/context/tool quality misses the acceptance suite |
    | Durable orchestration | PostgreSQL-backed worker with transactional leases, persisted step dependencies, timers, and inbox | Consider Temporal when operational evidence shows the custom workflow engine costs more than migration |
    | Computer | E2B adapter with scoped lifecycle and hardened access settings | Substitute another provider through the same interface if reliability/cost/control fails |
    | Browsing | Existing Playwright browser worker for controlled workflows | Evaluate browser-use if exploratory browsing quality justifies it |
    | Data | PostgreSQL for authoritative application state; private S3-compatible storage for artifacts | Add vector retrieval only after lexical retrieval and explicit memory prove insufficient |
    | Notifications | Persisted outbox plus push delivery | Push is a wake-up hint; clients always fetch authoritative state |
    | Diagnostics | Structured events, latency/cost metrics, redacted logs | Optional external observability only after its data handling is chosen |
    
    Use hosted model APIs in the prototype if configured by the team. No local-model constraint applies to this cloud phase. Pin model versions where possible and evaluate one strong tool-calling model before adding routing. Record model/provider data destinations and retention settings; do not imply confidentiality merely because an executor is isolated.
    
    **Thread-service decision:** the lowest-effort experiment may use CopilotKit Intelligence with clearly disclosed test data. Before the team alpha, either accept its service terms, cost, retention, deletion, and hosting model or replace its thread storage/replay integration with Me-owned persistence. Replacing it is engineering work, not an environment flag. Disable optional telemetry and optional external search integrations by default until intentionally configured.
    
    ## 4. The key behavior: only dependent work waits
    
    Represent a goal as a persisted directed acyclic graph of steps. Each step declares dependencies, required input references, output contract, capability, grants, budget, and completion check. Validate plans for cycles and invalid tool references. The LLM proposes the graph; deterministic code validates and schedules it.
    
    Example:
    
    ```text
    Goal: compare three products and design our agent
      A: research confirmed product              ready -> running -> done
      B: identify ambiguous product             waiting_input(question-1)
      C: compare open-source frameworks          ready -> running -> done
      D: draft reusable architecture             depends C -> ready -> done
      E: complete final comparison               depends A, B, D -> waiting
    ```
    
    The agent posts question-1 once, records what it blocks, and continues A/C/D. When an answer arrives from any device, the server stores an idempotent answer event, validates who may answer, invalidates affected assumptions, and wakes B. Unrelated completed work remains intact.
    
    Persist `Goal`, `TaskStep`, `Dependency`, `Question`, `Answer`, `Action`, `Approval`, `Artifact`, `Schedule`, and `Event`. Public step states: `ready`, `running`, `waiting_input`, `waiting_approval`, `blocked_dependency`, `succeeded`, `failed`, `cancelled`. Distinguish a temporarily blocked branch from a terminally failed goal.
    
    Questions identify affected steps and whether an answer is mandatory. Timeouts never count as approval. Optional questions can use a disclosed default; mandatory ones remain pending. Parent cancellation prevents all future branch dispatch. Limit concurrency per user and serialize writes to the same browser session, repository, or workspace.
    
    Follow-up messages are durable server records, not just client UI state. If a new instruction changes a running task, apply it at a safe checkpoint, increment the plan revision, and reevaluate affected grants. Show a partial result if all remaining branches need input. Do not keep spending model calls while every branch is waiting.
    
    ## 5. Remote computer lifecycle and boundaries
    
    Define a provider-neutral interface for create/attach, execute, file read/write, screenshot, preview, pause/resume, terminate, and export artifacts. Only the trusted control plane holds provider keys. Sandbox metadata and IDs must be bound to tenant, user, project, and environment; never trust an arbitrary sandbox ID from a client or model.
    
    Default: one sandbox per active task/project, with no cross-user reuse. Keep account browser profiles in a separate user-scoped service. Persist durable results in object storage; a sandbox is working state, not the only copy of a deliverable. Destroy temporary environments according to retention policy.
    
    Acquire execution leases while a job runs, heartbeat long operations, and pause idle environments when no active work needs them. A task running with the phone closed must not depend on a visible desktop tab refreshing its timeout. Extend the upstream short command budget with cancellable job handles and polling for builds/renders; do not merely raise every API request timeout.
    
    OpenMuse's [E2B adapter documentation](https://github.com/CopilotKit/openmuse/blob/a4944f4c471d3dc93b8bfc060b5da309b5216ab2/docs/COMPUTER.md) describes unrestricted outbound access, reachable listening ports, passwordless sudo inside the VM, and a desktop stream bearer URL. Its approval enforcement covers specific application connectors, while general desktop/network behavior partly relies on agent instructions. These are constraints of that integration, not universal limitations of E2B.
    
    Use the provider's [network controls](https://docs.e2b.dev/network/internet-access), protected ingress, and our own authenticated preview proxy where supported and verified. Never expose a raw development server containing task files. A domain allowlist alone cannot prevent an upload to an allowed domain or a form submission to a logged-in website.
    
    For the first alpha, keep arbitrary code/render environments offline after curated dependencies are installed. Use a separate controlled public-web research browser without personal login credentials. Execute email, calendar, upload, or publishing through typed, approval-enforced connectors. General logged-in autonomous GUI work is a later capability until its commitment boundary is demonstrable.
    
    [E2B persistence](https://docs.e2b.dev/sandbox/persistence) supports resumable sandboxes, but OpenMuse's inspected adapter deliberately uses filesystem-only pause, ending processes. Test the selected adapter's behavior rather than assuming a resumed browser, render, or command is still running. After recovery, reconstruct execution from recorded checkpoints and exported artifacts.
    
    ## 6. Capability delivery
    
    | Capability | Initial end-to-end implementation | Completion evidence |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | Research | Search/browse public sources, extract evidence, compare, write a report | Source URLs, retrieval times, report file, and a claims check |
    | Code/debug | Import explicit repository snapshot, inspect, edit, run tests, bounded repair, produce patch and preview | Source/diff, actual test output, authenticated preview where applicable |
    | Animation | Brief -> storyboard -> Manim source -> draft render -> frame review -> repair -> final output | Editable source, playable MP4, render output, duration/resolution and content checks |
    | Documents | Read permitted attachments, extract structured information, create an output | Artifact and source references; review before external transfer |
    | Personal memory | Explicit preferences, project decisions, authorized retrieval, correction/deletion | User can inspect the memory and identify its source/scope |
    | Scheduled work | Explicit schedule creates ordinary budgeted tasks | Schedule history, disable action, deduplicated outcomes |
    
    Start animation with Manim and templates; add Motion Canvas/other renderers through the same worker. Treat Remotion as a separately evaluated adapter because commercial use has specific terms. Generative image/video models add separate provider and resource choices; they are not necessary for useful programmatic animation.
    
    General-purpose capability comes from composing a small set of reliable tools. One primary agent is enough initially. Add specialists only when evaluations show an advantage; all delegation inherits narrower grants, scoped context, resource limits, and cancellation.
    
    ## 7. Identity, permissions, memory, and recovery
    
    Create real tenant/user/project identities before shared team access. Default projects and memories to private; shared projects require explicit membership. Enforce identity at task reads/writes, retrieval, browser/profile access, artifact downloads, notifications, thread replay, and sandbox attachment. A shared access key and a per-user sandbox are not sufficient account isolation.
    
    Keep connector credentials in a secret broker. Give tool workers only task-scoped grants and data. Model keys, cloud control-plane keys, database credentials, and unrelated account tokens never enter a general execution environment. Never use one logged-in browser profile for all team members.
    
    The tool broker deterministically allows, denies, or creates a review request. Approval binds actor, task/step, action type, canonical arguments, recipients/destination, payload/artifact hashes, policy revision, expiry, and one-time execution state. Approval of a plan does not grant arbitrary later mutations. Tool results and webpage content cannot authorize new actions.
    
    Persist action intent before dispatch. Use connector idempotency keys where available; otherwise reconcile uncertain outcomes instead of automatically retrying. Crash recovery and duplicate notification taps must not cause duplicate sends, purchases, or publications. Cancellation halts future work, terminates applicable jobs, and reports external operations already dispatched.
    
    Memory is separate from task checkpoints. Store explicit preferences, user/project scope, source, timestamps, retention, and provenance. Authorize before retrieval and include scope in cache keys. Provide edit/forget/export flows; propagate deletion through derived summaries, indexes, thread services, and backups according to disclosed retention. Add embeddings only after retrieval tests show a need.
    
    Use client event cursors and a transactional notification outbox. Reconnect fetches current state plus missing events. Push notifications contain minimal information and open an authenticated task; losing or duplicating a push must not lose or repeat work. The database is the authority for tasks, questions, approvals, and results.
    
    ## 8. Repository responsibilities
    
    | Repository | Cloud-phase responsibility |
    | --- | --- |
    | `agentic-framework` | Harness interface, step graph/scheduler, capability definitions, broker, memory access, execution adapters, evaluations |
    | `backend-server` | Account/project access, external API, durable inbox, approvals, artifact authorization, event delivery and notification outbox |
    | `infra-server` | Cloud deployment, PostgreSQL/object storage, worker operations, sandbox lifecycle, ingress/egress, secrets, monitoring, backup/restore |
    | `phone-app` | Adapt reused Expo screens: goals/chat, branch progress, questions, approvals, previews, notifications, settings |
    | `web-app` | Existing public site; add a clearly labeled cloud-prototype entry only when the product description and authenticated experience are ready |
    
    Avoid immediately scattering an imported OpenMuse monorepo across all these repositories. First use an isolated checkout to validate the complete upstream path. Then extract reusable runtime/domain modules and client components with preserved license notices and recorded upstream revision. Define one canonical schema for tasks/events/approvals; do not duplicate it across backends.
    
    API operations: submit goal, read task/steps, submit follow-up, answer question, resolve approval, cancel task, stream/replay events, fetch artifact, edit memory, and manage schedules. Mutations use idempotency keys; responses include tenant-scoped IDs and schema versions. Internal model traces and raw reasoning are not user-facing progress.
    
    ## 9. Phased implementation and decision gates
    
    Estimate: three engineers covering runtime, platform/tools, and client/backend; approximately 8–12 weeks to a constrained internal multi-user alpha if upstream reuse works. These are planning estimates, not measured delivery commitments. Authentication, dependency-service replacement, and execution constraints may extend the schedule.
    
    | Phase | Estimate | Deliverables and exit gate |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | 0: live feasibility | 3–5 working days | Pin upstream, run with synthetic data, real model, PostgreSQL, and remote computer; close client and verify task continuation. Inventory actual external data paths and cost. Decide thread-service policy and whether to keep the harness. |
    | 1: independent task | Weeks 2–3 | Me-owned task/event contract, durable follow-up inbox, dependency graph, separate leased worker, artifact export, reconnect flow. One question blocks one branch while another finishes. |
    | 2: team boundary | Weeks 4–5 | Accounts, project membership, tenant-scoped storage, sandbox mapping, budget enforcement, broker/approvals, authenticated previews. Two users cannot access each other's tasks/files/profiles. No shared deployment is opened to a team before this gate. |
    | 3: useful capabilities | Weeks 6–8 | Research reports, coding/test/repair workflow, animation render/revise/export, push notifications, explicit schedules, editable memory. Verify real outputs with the app offline. |
    | 4: reliable alpha | Weeks 9–12 if needed | Restart/reconciliation drills, dependency outages, retention/delete/export, restore, cost controls, held-out task tests, onboarding and operational runbook. |
    
    Use web first to shorten the runtime feedback loop, then exercise a signed iOS development build on a real device before claiming iOS background-task acceptance. JavaScript exports and simulator recordings do not establish push delivery or signed native installation.
    
    ### First tickets
    
    1. **CF-001 — Feasibility checkout:** pin upstream and record live task/model/E2B/thread-service results. Deliver a keep/adapt/replace decision; no migration by assumption.
    2. **CF-002 — Canonical task contracts:** define task, step dependency, question/answer, grant/approval, event, artifact, and sandbox ownership records.
    3. **CF-003 — Durable non-blocking scheduler:** persist ready/waiting branches, transactional claims, answer wake-up, branch cancellation, plan revisions, and resource limits.
    4. **CF-004 — Cloud execution adapter:** authenticated sandbox mapping, offline code worker, job lifecycle, artifact export, pause/resume, protected previews, and cleanup.
    5. **CF-005 — Team authentication:** real sessions, membership, scoped retrieval/storage/thread access, artifact ownership, and revocation.
    6. **CF-006 — Enforced external actions:** broker, stored review, credential scoping, action ledger, idempotency/reconciliation, and execution-time policy checks.
    7. **CF-007 — Remote-control client:** goal submission, branch progress, durable questions/answers, approvals, artifacts, reconnect/replay, and cancel.
    8. **CF-008 — Capability packs:** research, coding/debugging, and animation with task-specific result checks.
    9. **CF-009 — Personal continuity:** authorized memory, explicit schedules, durable notifications, native push, and user-configurable budgets.
    10. **CF-010 — Alpha operations:** measured quality suite, failure injection, restore/update rollback, deletion/retention, diagnostics, and spend monitoring.
    
    CF-002 follows the feasibility decision. Scheduler and execution work can then proceed alongside client and identity implementation. Team access depends on CF-005; connected-account commitments depend on CF-006. Broader capabilities depend on working artifacts and task recovery, rather than just new prompts.
    
    ## 10. Acceptance suite and costs
    
    The first acceptance scenario is: submit a research goal, terminate the app, let the remote worker finish, reopen to the persisted report, and receive a notification where permissions allow. The stronger scenario is: one branch asks a question, another creates an artifact, the worker restarts, and an answer from a second client resumes only the blocked branch.
    
    Before internal alpha, maintain at least 40 versioned normal tasks plus independent failure/permission fixtures. Proposed targets: at least 80% independently checked completion on supported tasks, with per-capability results and intervention counts reported. Broader general-purpose claims require broader evaluation.
    
    Mandatory scenarios: duplicated answer/approval events; expired grant; changed action arguments; cross-user object IDs; browser session/profile leakage; public preview access; raw network bypass; prompt injection; sandbox expiry; model timeout; worker lease expiry; stop during a render; disconnect/reconnect; failed push; and crash after a service accepts an external action.
    
    Persist task state before acknowledgment; no accepted goal may disappear after restart. Measure p50/p95 time to first progress, completion time, queue delay, retries, and recovery time on the declared deployment. Test both live-model tasks and deterministic fixtures, labeling each. Record what was actually run, rather than copying upstream test counts.
    
    Track variable cost per verified completed task:
    
    ```text
    model input/output + sandbox active time + browser time
    + artifact storage/egress + search/API fees + retry overhead
    + allocated API/worker/database/thread-service cost
    ```
    
    Also measure failed-task cost and idle infrastructure spend. Set per-task token/time/compute caps, per-user concurrency, daily/monthly spend limits, render quotas, and idle cleanup. An always-available agent should wait cheaply when idle or awaiting input; it need not run model inference continuously.
    
    Do not choose hardware commitments or subscription pricing before measuring actual provider usage. Provider prices and limits must be checked again when provisioning; no price estimate is assumed here.
    
    ## 11. When to add another framework
    
    Keep the built-in harness if it passes research, code-repair, animation, context, and permission tests. If it fails because of agent-loop limitations, compare it with Deep Agents using the same tasks/tools/model and integrate the winner behind the harness interface. Do not rewrite a working task engine just to change a model loop.
    
    Keep the SQL worker if leases, timers, input/approval waits, dependency graphs, cancellation, and reconciliation remain understandable and tested. Add Temporal if long-running workflow evolution, operational recovery, or distributed coordination becomes a measured burden. A migration must assign one owner for durable scheduling; do not run two competing state machines for the same action. [Temporal activities](https://docs.temporal.io/activities) still require idempotency and explicit side-effect handling.
    
    OpenBot is a desktop-oriented reference, rather than the main starting point for this remote-first phase. Its current [README](https://github.com/nightly-labs/openbot) documents broad execution privileges, so its execution policy should not be inherited as Me's approval model. OpenClaw/Hermes remain alternative complete assistants if OpenMuse integration costs exceed the reuse benefit.
    
    The immediate next deliverable is a reproducible feasibility result and architecture decision, followed by one complete remote task path. Infrastructure creation, live account connections, public publishing, and paid provider use are implementation steps, not actions performed by this planning document.

    # Me product architecture
    
    Canonical product understanding, based on the user's clarification on 2026-11-02. This document supersedes contradictory hosting assumptions in the earlier personal-agent plans. It describes intended boundaries; the runtime repositories are currently bootstrap repositories.
    
    ## Confirmed deployment model
    
    Me is a personal/family agent that runs on a separate computer in the user's home. The user can buy that computer or use a suitable spare computer they already own. The phone is the interface to the agent. Me operates a hosted backend that connects the phone experience with the user's home infrastructure.
    
    Independent execution means the home computer can continue work when the phone app is closed or offline. It does not mean the agent is hosted in Me's cloud, and it does not require controlling the user's everyday laptop or desktop. A spare computer intentionally provisioned as the home host becomes the agent's dedicated execution environment.
    
    ```mermaid
    flowchart TD
      User[User] --> Phone[phone-app: agent interface]
      Phone <-->|Authenticated application connection| Backend[backend-server: hosted by Me]
      Backend <-->|Authenticated home connection| Home[infra-server: user's home computer]
      Setup[setup-infra: installer and maintenance tooling] --> Home
      Home --> Agent[agentic-framework: agent runtime]
      Agent --> Models[Model inference]
      Agent --> Tools[Browser, isolated code and render workers, integrations]
      Home --> Data[Local task state, memory, files and artifacts]
      Tools --> External[External services within approved scope]
    ```
    
    The connection shown is logical; transport, relay protocol, encryption design, and remote-access implementation are engineering decisions still to be made.
    
    ## Repository responsibilities
    
    | Repository | Where it runs | Responsibility |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | `phone-app` | User's phone | Agent conversations, tasks, progress, clarification answers, approvals, results, household controls, and home pairing |
    | `backend-server` | Me's hosted infrastructure | Application API, user/account identity, home registration and access, phone-to-home coordination, and notification delivery; exact relay/storage boundaries require design |
    | `infra-server` | User's separate home computer | Home service/API, authenticated connection with our backend, lifecycle of local agent and execution services, local persistence, resource management, and health |
    | `agentic-framework` | Within the user's home environment | Agent planning, model/tool integration, capability execution, task dependencies, clarification behavior, memory access, permissions, and task recovery |
    | `setup-infra` | During installation/maintenance on the home computer | Prerequisite/hardware checks, installation, configuration, registration/pairing, service startup, upgrades, diagnostics, and recovery tooling |
    | `web-app` | Public website hosting | Explain the product and provide the existing showcase/waitlist; later onboarding links can connect to the phone/setup experience |
    | `feed-algorithm` | Placement to be finalized | Feed ranking, goal controls, and ranking evaluation; access to personal context must be explicit |
    
    `setup-infra` prepares and maintains the home deployment; `infra-server` operates it. `agentic-framework` is the execution engine used there, rather than another public hosted backend. Browser, coding, and animation capabilities should run in isolated environments on the home host by default.
    
    ## A request through the system
    
    1. The user submits a request from `phone-app` to our hosted `backend-server`.
    2. The backend authenticates the user, resolves the authorized home installation, and delivers the request through its authenticated home connection.
    3. `infra-server` verifies the request and access scope, persists the home task, and hands execution to `agentic-framework`.
    4. The framework plans and executes using the home's configured model, memory, files, browser, and isolated workers.
    5. Progress, questions, approvals, and artifact references return through the backend to the phone. Proposed default: transfer private content only as necessary for the authenticated user experience, with explicit retention and encryption rules.
    6. Closing the app does not cancel an accepted task. The home worker keeps running while its machine and required services are available.
    7. A missing answer pauses dependent work. Independent steps continue. Answers and approvals are persisted at home and can resume execution when delivered.
    
    The phone should distinguish a request accepted by the hosted backend from one durably accepted by the home system. If delivery is queued while the home is offline, show that state rather than claiming execution has started.
    
    ## Design defaults to validate
    
    These are recommendations derived from the deployment model, not additional confirmed user requirements.
    
    - **Home authority:** store authoritative agent task state, personal memory, artifacts, execution receipts, and action approvals at home. Keep hosted account/routing state separate. Specify any hosted message queue retention explicitly.
    - **Outbound home connection:** let the home establish a persistent authenticated connection to the backend, avoiding a requirement that ordinary users expose a public home port. Select and validate the transport separately.
    - **Durable messaging:** use request/event IDs, acknowledgments, replay cursors, and duplicate handling. Reconnects must not duplicate a task or approved external action.
    - **Local permission enforcement:** the home checks actor, device, household rules, capability, and exact approved action before execution. Cloud routing alone must not grant arbitrary host shell access.
    - **Hardware flexibility:** publish a validated minimum configuration and capability tiers. Model inference, browser sessions, code builds, and rendering contend for the same home resources; queue and budget them.
    - **Local-first model behavior:** preserve the website's intent of private processing at home. Any external model option must be separately specified and disclosed; execution hosting and model-provider selection are distinct decisions.
    - **Private relay design:** decide whether private payloads are encrypted end to end between paired phones and the home. Hosting a relay does not by itself establish that Me cannot read content. Do not make that claim before implementing and validating the key lifecycle.
    - **Isolated execution:** provide scoped workspaces for generated code and rendering; keep account credentials, home service keys, and unrelated household files out of them.
    - **Recoverable setup:** installation should be rerunnable, detect existing deployments, preserve data on upgrades, and offer an explicit backup/restore path. Reinstalling the runtime must not silently erase personal memory.
    
    ## Availability and ownership
    
    | Condition | Intended behavior |
    | --- | --- |
    | Phone closed/offline | Home execution continues; the phone retrieves progress/results on reconnect |
    | Home powered off/asleep | Agent execution is unavailable; backend/client show home offline and any pending delivery honestly |
    | Home internet disconnected | Local work can continue where its dependencies allow; remote coordination and internet tools wait/retry according to policy |
    | Hosted backend unavailable | Already accepted independent home work can continue; phone communication through that backend is unavailable until recovery |
    | Home restarts | Persisted tasks recover; uncertain external effects reconcile instead of blindly replaying |
    
    A home-hosted agent is not automatically always available. Setup must explain power/sleep behavior, storage, updates, and recovery. There is no implicit cloud executor taking over when the home is offline.
    
    ## Consequences for the framework evaluation
    
    Evaluate reusable agent software for installation on user-owned home hardware, useful local-model operation, persistent execution, browser/code/animation capability, enforceable permissions, remote progress/approval APIs, resource limits, and upgrades.
    
    OpenMuse remains a possible interface/workflow reference; its hosted services and remote-computer adapter do not establish fit for this deployment. Deep Agents, Hermes, OpenClaw, and other candidates remain options to test. No final framework selection has been made through an executed comparison.
    
    Do not make E2B, a cloud computer, Temporal, or a hosted thread service mandatory merely because they appeared in an earlier draft. Reuse is valuable only where it fits the home-hosted product and the hosted-backend boundary.
    
    ## First implementation milestone
    
    Establish the actual deployment path before expanding capabilities:
    
    1. `setup-infra` installs and starts a minimal `infra-server` on a test home computer and pairs it to the hosted backend.
    2. `phone-app` submits an authenticated task through `backend-server`.
    3. The home persists and executes that task through an initial agent runtime, then returns a saved artifact and progress events.
    4. Close/reopen the phone, disconnect/reconnect the home connection, and restart the home service. Verify task identity, recovery, and delivery without duplicated execution.
    5. Add one persisted clarification and one approval-controlled action. Verify independent work continues while only the dependent branch waits.
    
    This is the shared product model to use when refining the end-to-end implementation plan across all repositories.

## Assistant

Yes—I incorrectly equated “independent” with cloud-hosted. **The agent runs on a separate computer in the user’s home, and our hosted backend connects the phone to it.**

```text
phone-app
    ↕
backend-server — hosted by us
    ↕
infra-server — hosted on the user’s home computer
    ├── agentic-framework
    ├── models, browser, code and animation execution
    └── local memory, tasks, files and results

setup-infra → installs and maintains the home environment
```

The repo boundaries are:

| Repo | Role |
|---|---|
| `phone-app` | User interface for conversations, tasks, approvals, progress, and results |
| `backend-server` | Our hosted API, identity, home registration, and communication coordination |
| `infra-server` | Service running on the home computer that operates the local agent environment |
| `agentic-framework` | Agent planning, tools, capabilities, permissions, and persistent execution |
| `setup-infra` | Prepares a purchased or spare computer: prerequisites, installation, configuration, pairing, and upgrades |

The agent continues when the phone closes **because the home computer keeps working**. If that computer is offline, agent execution is unavailable until it returns.

This means framework selection must fit user-owned home hardware and our remote communication flow. Cloud computers are no longer the default foundation.

I recorded this in the [canonical product architecture](/Users/kgensupertramp/Desktop/me/agentic-framework/docs/product-architecture.md) and marked the conflicting earlier plans accordingly.

    +## Household data and multiple sessions
    +
    +Confirmed requirements: the home stores users' conversations and other personal data, supports multiple household users, and supports multiple chat sessions. The structure and isolation rules below are proposed implementation defaults.
    +
    +```text
    +Home installation
    +  Household membership and shared resources
    +  User A
    +    Private profile, memories, files and connected accounts
    +    Conversation 1 -> messages, attachments, tasks and results
    +    Conversation 2 -> messages, attachments, tasks and results
    +  User B
    +    Private profile, memories, files and connected accounts
    +    Conversation 3 -> messages, attachments, tasks and results
    +  Explicitly shared household/project spaces
    +  Shared model service and bounded worker capacity
    +```
    +
    +A user, phone/device, conversation, task, and model invocation are different identities. One user can have multiple devices and conversations; one conversation can contain multiple tasks; a task can continue after its originating session disconnects. Use stable IDs and explicit links rather than using a single session ID for all of them.
    +
    +The home data service should own conversation messages, attachments, user settings, memory, task state, approvals, artifacts, authorized browser/account state, and derived indexes. Treat checkpoints, caches, logs, and backups as potentially sensitive data too. Hosted account identity and routing metadata remain separate from this authoritative home data. Any cloud buffering or content retention must be specified explicitly.
    +
    +Recommended access defaults:
    +
    +- Conversations, personal memory, files, browser profiles, and connected accounts belong to a user and are private unless explicitly shared. Shared storage hardware does not imply shared access.
    +- Shared household facts and collaborative projects use explicit membership and visibility rules. Do not mix every family member's context into one prompt or vector index without authorization filters.
    +- Define guardian powers and chat visibility as an explicit product policy. Being the household administrator must not silently imply access to all private chats. Protection from a machine administrator with physical/root access is a separate threat-model decision.
    +- Enforce scope on the home at retrieval, prompt construction, task execution, artifact access, event replay, notifications, caches, and exports. A user ID in model-generated text is not an authenticated identity.
    +- Give each conversation its own history and task context. Retrieve authorized cross-conversation memory deliberately; do not copy every conversation into every prompt.
    +
    +One shared model service can process requests from multiple conversations; separate users do not inherently require separate model copies or always-running agents. Each run must construct an isolated context, and any reused model/KV cache must remain correctly scoped. Hardware determines how much work can execute simultaneously; supporting concurrent sessions includes fairly queuing work when capacity is exhausted.
    +
    +Use per-user and per-task limits, prioritize interactive replies over long renders where appropriate, and prevent one user's workload from monopolizing the home. Serialize conflicting operations on the same conversation, browser profile, repository, or file. Use versions/transactions for concurrent memory and document updates rather than silently overwriting another run's changes.

## Assistant

Exactly. **The home computer is the household’s persistent AI and data server.**

It hosts:

- **Multiple users:** each family member has their own identity, preferences, memory, and connected accounts.
- **Multiple conversations per user:** separate histories, attachments, task context, and results.
- **Background tasks:** work continues independently of an open chat or connected phone.
- **Household sharing:** explicitly shared files, knowledge, and collaborative spaces.
- **Shared compute:** models, browsers, coding workers, and animation rendering serve those users within the computer’s capacity.

The proposed structure is:

```text
Home computer
├── Household membership and permissions
├── User A
│   ├── Personal data and memory
│   ├── Conversation 1 → tasks and results
│   └── Conversation 2 → tasks and results
├── User B
│   ├── Personal data and memory
│   └── Conversations → tasks and results
├── Explicitly shared household data
└── Shared model service and execution workers
```

**Sharing the computer must not automatically share everyone’s conversations.** Private versus shared access—and parental supervision—needs explicit rules.

We can share model resources while keeping each conversation’s context isolated. Multiple sessions can remain active even when the hardware needs to queue their execution.

I’ve added these requirements to the [canonical architecture](/Users/kgensupertramp/Desktop/me/agentic-framework/docs/product-architecture.md), including concurrent sessions, data isolation, persistence, and household resource scheduling.

    - **Isolated execution:** provide scoped workspaces for generated code and rendering; keep account credentials, home service keys, and unrelated household files out of them.
    - **Recoverable setup:** installation should be rerunnable, detect existing deployments, preserve data on upgrades, and offer an explicit backup/restore path. Reinstalling the runtime must not silently erase personal memory.
    
    ## Availability and ownership
    
    | Condition | Intended behavior |
    | --- | --- |
    | Phone closed/offline | Home execution continues; the phone retrieves progress/results on reconnect |
    | Home powered off/asleep | Agent execution is unavailable; backend/client show home offline and any pending delivery honestly |
    | Home internet disconnected | Local work can continue where its dependencies allow; remote coordination and internet tools wait/retry according to policy |
    | Hosted backend unavailable | Already accepted independent home work can continue; phone communication through that backend is unavailable until recovery |
    | Home restarts | Persisted tasks recover; uncertain external effects reconcile instead of blindly replaying |
    
    A home-hosted agent is not automatically always available. Setup must explain power/sleep behavior, storage, updates, and recovery. There is no implicit cloud executor taking over when the home is offline.
    
    ## Consequences for the framework evaluation
    
    Evaluate reusable agent software for installation on user-owned home hardware, useful local-model operation, persistent execution, browser/code/animation capability, enforceable permissions, multiple users and isolated conversations, remote progress/approval APIs, fair resource limits, and upgrades. Single-owner tools require additional isolation work before serving a family; multiple chat tabs alone do not establish multi-user support.
    
    OpenMuse remains a possible interface/workflow reference; its hosted services and remote-computer adapter do not establish fit for this deployment. Deep Agents, Hermes, OpenClaw, and other candidates remain options to test. No final framework selection has been made through an executed comparison.
    
    Do not make E2B, a cloud computer, Temporal, or a hosted thread service mandatory merely because they appeared in an earlier draft. Reuse is valuable only where it fits the home-hosted product and the hosted-backend boundary.
    
    ## First implementation milestone
    
    Establish the actual deployment path before expanding capabilities:
    
    1. `setup-infra` installs and starts a minimal `infra-server` on a test home computer and pairs it to the hosted backend.
    2. `phone-app` submits an authenticated task through `backend-server`.
    3. The home persists and executes that task through an initial agent runtime, then returns a saved artifact and progress events.
    4. Close/reopen the phone, disconnect/reconnect the home connection, and restart the home service. Verify task identity, recovery, and delivery without duplicated execution.
    5. Add one persisted clarification and one approval-controlled action. Verify independent work continues while only the dependent branch waits.
    6. Create two household users with two conversations each. Submit overlapping tasks, confirm isolated history/memory/files/account state, test explicit sharing, and verify queued workloads progress fairly. Restart the home and reconnect each user without mixing events or results.
    
    This is the shared product model to use when refining the end-to-end implementation plan across all repositories.
