    # Me whole-product delivery plan
    
    Status: proposed cross-repository implementation plan, 2026-11-02. Product requirements and deployment boundaries are recorded in [product architecture](product-architecture.md). This plan does not select a final agent framework or claim an implemented system.
    
    ## Working principle
    
    Develop one integrated product across the repositories. A feature is complete when the user can install the required home services, access it from the phone through our hosted backend, use it with the correct identity and permissions, recover from interruptions, and retrieve its persisted result.
    
    Evaluate open-source agent reuse against that complete path. A successful standalone framework demo is useful evidence, but it is not a completed Me feature. Treat `infra-server` as a first-class product service throughout runtime development, rather than deployment work deferred until afterward.
    
    ## Responsibilities that must stay distinct
    
    | Area | Primary owner | Collaborators |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | Account identity, home registration, authenticated routing | `backend-server` | `phone-app`, `infra-server`, `setup-infra` |
    | Household membership enforcement, conversation/history service, local data and artifact access | `infra-server` | `backend-server`, `phone-app`, `agentic-framework` |
    | Accepted-job lifecycle, durable dispatch, worker supervision, resource scheduling, home health | `infra-server` | `agentic-framework`, `setup-infra` |
    | Agent plan, step dependencies, model context, tool selection, task-specific completion checks | `agentic-framework` | `infra-server`, `phone-app` |
    | Household policy administration and durable approval records | `infra-server` | `phone-app`, `backend-server`, `agentic-framework` |
    | Enforcement immediately before a tool runs | Home tool broker, defined with `infra-server` and `agentic-framework` | Execution workers |
    | Installation, prerequisites, service configuration, upgrade/recovery tooling | `setup-infra` | `infra-server`, `agentic-framework`, `backend-server` |
    | Conversation/task experience, onboarding, questions, approvals, results and controls | `phone-app` | All runtime services |
    | Goal-driven feed ranking and evaluation | `feed-algorithm` | `infra-server`, `phone-app` |
    | Public explanation, waitlist, supported-hardware/setup guidance | `web-app` | `setup-infra`, product |
    
    The home job manager owns whether a run is accepted, queued, active, cancelled, or recovered. The agent owns the plan and execution state inside that run. Use one durable authority for each transition; do not create independent schedulers that both believe they can retry or dispatch the same action.
    
    Conversations and personal data are home-service records accessed through authorized interfaces. A selected framework may keep its own versioned internal checkpoints, but must not become the only way to read/export a person's conversation history. The hosted backend owns delivery/routing state, not an independent copy of the home task lifecycle.
    
    ## Interfaces to define before implementation fans out
    
    1. **Phone ↔ hosted backend:** sessions, household/home selection, conversation/task requests, acknowledgments, event replay, questions/approvals, and artifact access. Separate hosted acceptance, home acceptance, and actual execution.
    2. **Hosted backend ↔ home:** authenticated connection establishment, installation/device identity, message envelopes, authorization scope, request IDs, acknowledgments, ordering/replay, expiry, reconnect, and revocation behavior. Specify private-payload encryption and any hosted buffer retention.
    3. **Home ↔ agent runtime:** start/resume/cancel a run with trusted identity, scoped context references, input/answer references, capability grants, budgets, checkpoint references, progress events, and artifact declarations. Do not pass unrestricted database or host access.
    4. **Home ↔ execution workers:** resource request, isolated workspace, credential/network scope, job handle, heartbeat, logs, output/artifact export, cancellation, and cleanup.
    5. **Installer ↔ home release:** supported platform/hardware profile, versioned configuration, data directories, service health/readiness, migration prerequisites, backup/restore, and upgrade/rollback compatibility.
    6. **Feed ↔ household data:** explicit authorized goals/preferences and content inputs, ranking output, user controls, and evaluation; no blanket access to private conversations.
    
    Publish versioned schemas once and consume generated bindings where practical. Choose the authoritative contract package/location in the first architecture decision; avoid hand-copied schemas across repositories. Mixed phone/backend/home versions are normal and need explicit compatibility rules and capability negotiation.
    
    ## Build in end-to-end milestones
    
    | Milestone | Product behavior | Work across repositories | Completion evidence |
    | --- | --- | --- | --- |
    | M0: system contracts | One agreed identity, data, lifecycle, and transport model | Define contracts, threat/data boundaries, hardware test profile, deployment responsibilities, and framework experiment | Recorded decisions, sample messages, failure cases, and one-owner-per-state map |
    | M1: install and pair | A user provisions a test home computer and sees it online from the phone | Setup checks/starts home; home registers/connects; hosted backend authenticates/routes; phone pairs/displays health | Fresh installation, repeat installation, unauthorized pairing rejection, reconnect, and honest offline state |
    | M2: private conversation | Two users each hold multiple persistent chats | Home data/schema/access controls; phone conversation UI; hosted request/event delivery; basic agent/model adapter | History survives restarts; scoped retrieval and replay prevent mixing users/conversations |
    | M3: independent task | An accepted task continues after closing the phone and returns an artifact | Home queue/worker supervision; agent execution/checkpoints; setup worker prerequisites; phone events/results | App closure, home connection loss, service restart, task recovery, and authenticated artifact retrieval |
    | M4: questions and approvals | One branch waits for input while independent work continues; approved actions execute once | Agent dependency plan; home durable inbox/approval broker; hosted delivery; phone interaction | Answer from another session; duplicate/expired/changed approval rejection; uncertain-action reconciliation |
    | M5: real capabilities | Research, code/debug, and animation workflows produce verified outputs | Agent skills/tools; home browser/code/render workers and budgets; installer dependencies; phone preview/export | Sources/report, patch with actual test results, editable animation with checked render |
    | M6: household continuity | Members use private/shared memory and explicit schedules without monopolizing the computer | Home memberships/sharing/queue/retention; agent memory/schedules; phone controls; hosted notifications | Two users with overlapping runs, explicit sharing, revocation, fair queues, deletion/export, schedule cancellation |
    | M7: product alpha | A household can maintain and recover the installation | Setup updates/restore; home health/storage/diagnostics; backend compatibility; phone onboarding/help; public guidance | Data-preserving upgrade, recovery on a clean host, resource-pressure tests, supportable onboarding |
    | M8: feed integration | Family controls change a goal-aligned feed under declared data permissions | Feed ranking/evaluation; home data contract; phone feed/controls; content/network integration decisions | Ranking/control fixtures and privacy/access tests; measured relevance and resource use |
    
    M1–M4 form the first integrated prototype. Do not wait for sophisticated coding or animation before validating installation, multi-user storage, request delivery, and restart behavior. Conversely, do not call M1–M4 a completed general-purpose agent: real capability quality is measured in M5.
    
    Some work can proceed concurrently after contracts stabilize, but releases cross the same milestone gate. No repo may claim the product feature complete solely because its own endpoint or screen exists. Use linked work items in the participating repositories and a single feature-level acceptance record.
    
    ## Example: animation is a whole-product feature
    
    For “make a 20-second fractions animation,” the phone submits the brief and displays progress; the backend routes it to the correct home/user; the home persists the task, allocates resources, and creates an isolated workspace; the agent generates and revises scenes/code; the render worker produces output; the home stores source and video with ownership; and the phone previews/downloads the result. Setup must install compatible renderer dependencies. Cancellation, low disk space, restart, and another user's concurrent chat must also behave correctly.
    
    This same feature checklist applies to research, browsing, coding, document work, and future integrations.
    
    ## Home infrastructure work to design alongside the agent
    
    - **Data:** household/users, conversations/messages, attachments, tasks/runs, approvals, memory, artifacts, browser profiles, logs, derived indexes, retention and backups. Separate framework checkpoint internals from product records.
    - **Compute:** shared model lifecycle, interactive requests, context isolation, worker pools, per-user quotas, render/build queues, process limits, cancellation and resource-pressure behavior.
    - **Execution:** scoped files, isolated generated code, browser ownership, secret brokerage, destination/action permissions, dependency installation and artifact validation.
    - **Connectivity:** outbound authenticated home connection, device keys, pairing/revocation, reconnect/replay, delivery acknowledgment, offline queue expiry and minimal notification payloads.
    - **Operations:** readiness versus liveness, disk/capacity visibility, sleep/reboot behavior, worker recovery, safe diagnostics, release compatibility, migrations and restore drills.
    
    Specific technologies, supported operating systems, encryption/key lifecycle, household-admin visibility, hardware tiers, and backup destinations remain decisions to validate. Record assumptions visibly instead of treating them as already confirmed product requirements.
    
    ## Cross-repository acceptance and change discipline
    
    For every feature, record its user outcome, participating repos, contract/schema changes, data ownership, permissions, worker requirements, resource budget, interruption behavior, installation/migration impact, and end-to-end acceptance evidence. Scale this record to the feature; a small change need not produce a large document.
    
    Build a development integration environment containing a hosted-backend instance, a separate simulated home instance with persistent storage, an agent worker, and a client. Keep real home-hardware acceptance as a distinct check. Tests must be able to interrupt the phone connection, backend/home connection, worker, and home service independently.
    
    Key system cases: two users with multiple chats, duplicate request delivery, out-of-order/replayed events, expired membership/grants, home offline at submit time, backend outage during a local task, worker crash, low storage, model/renderer failure, untrusted tool content, and recovery after an uncertain external write.
    
    Release manifests should identify compatible backend/home/agent/installer/client contract versions. Stage changes so older clients/homes receive an explicit supported response. Back up before destructive schema migrations; rollback must respect data-schema compatibility rather than merely swapping executable versions.
    
    ## Immediate next deliverable
    
    Complete M0 as a small system design package: canonical contracts and IDs, data/identity map, home service decomposition, connection/acknowledgment sequence, installer/release manifest, and an M1–M4 acceptance script. In parallel with that design, evaluate a minimal agent adapter inside the proposed home boundary using the same identity/data/tool contracts.
    
    The framework decision must follow evidence from that integrated experiment. No single framework, SDK, desktop app, or home installer determines the architecture of the whole product.

    Thank you for helping build privacy-first home AI. These guidelines apply across
    the organization unless a repository documents more specific instructions.
    
    ## Find work
    
    Search existing issues and pull requests first. Use `good first issue` and
    `help wanted` labels to find scoped tasks. Open an issue for a bug or proposal;
    use community discussions for questions and cross-repository design.
    Discuss architecture, dependencies, and user-facing behavior before a large change.
    
    ## Make a change
    
    1. Fork the repository and branch from `main`, for example `feat/device-pairing`.
    2. Follow its README for setup. Repositories without application code do not yet
       have a supported runtime or build command.
    3. Keep the change focused. Add appropriate tests and update documentation.
    4. Run `python3 scripts/check_repository.py` and the project's documented checks.
    5. Open a pull request describing the problem, solution, and validation.
    6. Respond to review and resolve discussion threads. Maintainers squash merge.
    
    Use descriptive PR titles, such as `feat: add device pairing` or
    `docs: explain local setup`. A title convention is encouraged, not enforced.
    Contributions are under the repository's license. No CLA or DCO is required
    at this stage. Include third-party attribution and do not contribute code you
    are not authorized to share.
    
    ## Privacy, safety, and accessibility
    
    Use synthetic data in issues, tests, screenshots, and examples. Do not upload
    household conversations, children's information, credentials, or production logs.
    Explain permission changes, network calls, storage, telemetry, and data retention.
    Aim for accessible interfaces and user control over agent actions.
    AI-assisted contributions receive the same review and testing as other changes;
    contributors remain responsible for correctness, provenance, and security.
    
    ## Security and conduct
    
    Do not disclose vulnerabilities in public issues. Use **Security → Report a
    vulnerability** in the affected repository and read SECURITY.md.
    Follow CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md in all community spaces.

-0,0 +1,276 @@\\n+### Interpreter\\n+\\n+An `eval` tool is available. It runs JavaScript in a persistent REPL.\\n+\\n+- State (variables, functions) persists across tool calls and across multiple turns for this conversation thread.\\n+- Top-level `await` works; Promises resolve before the call returns.\\n+- Runtime sandbox: no built-in filesystem, network, stdlib, or wall-clock APIs (`fetch`, `require`, `fs`, `process`, real `Date.now()` are unavailable or stubbed).\\n+- External side effects from inside the REPL are only reachable via the `tools.*` namespace documented in the API reference below.\\n+- Timeout: 5.0s per call. Memory: 64 MB total.\\n+- `console.log` output is captured and returned alongside the result.\\n+\\n+### Dispatching Subagents with `task`\\n+\\n+`task` is your primitive for running configured subagents from inside the\\n+JavaScript REPL. Your job here is to DISTRIBUTE work, not to do it yourself:\\n+write JavaScript that fans work out to subagents and assembles their results.\\n+You handle the orchestration - fan-out, filtering, deduplication, multi-stage\\n+flow, and synthesis - in plain JavaScript.\\n+\\n+#### The primitive\\n+\\n+```javascript\\n+await task({\\n+  description,      // full autonomous task prompt\\n+  subagentType,     // configured subagent name\\n+  label,            // optional short UI label for this dispatch\\n+  responseSchema,   // optional JSON Schema for structured output\\n+}); // -> Promise<unknown>\\n+```\\n+\\n+`task` runs a full agentic loop for the selected configured subagent. The\\n+subagent can use whatever tools it was configured with, iterate, inspect\\n+context, and return one final result. `subagentType` is required; use one of\\n+the configured subagent names.\\n+\\n+`description` is the only prompt the subagent receives for this dispatch. Make\\n+it complete: the goal, the constraints, what to inspect, and the exact shape\\n+or level of detail you expect back. Give context as locators — file paths and\\n+symbol names — not as pasted file contents. If you already read a file while\\n+exploring, still pass its path and let the subagent read it; do not paste back\\n+what you read. Each dispatch is stateless from the caller's perspective; you\\n+cannot send follow-up messages to the same subagent run.\\n+\\n+`label` is optional: when provided, it is shown in the live progress UI\\n+instead of the default description-derived fallback. It is not sent to the\\n+subagent and does not affect execution.\\n+\\n+`responseSchema` is optional, but set it on any dispatch whose result feeds\\n+later code. A deterministic, typed shape is what lets you compose the next\\n+stage reliably — index it, sort it, compare fields, branch on it, merge it —\\n+instead of parsing free-form text. This is what makes a whole workflow\\n+composable as one script. When provided, the resolved value is already a typed\\n+JavaScript value matching the schema; do not call `JSON.parse` unless the\\n+subagent intentionally returned a JSON string. Dynamic schemas work for\\n+declarative subagents; runnable-backed subagents reject dynamic schemas because\\n+their runnable is already compiled.\\n+\\n+#### Approval model\\n+\\n+`task` dispatches from inside the already-running `eval` call. It\\n+does not route through the parent agent's `ToolNode`-managed `task` tool and\\n+does not trigger parent-level `interrupt_on` / HITL approval for each dispatch.\\n+Declarative subagents still honor approval middleware configured inside their\\n+own spec. If you need approval before launching a subagent from the parent, use\\n+the normal `task` tool outside JavaScript or ensure the `eval` call\\n+itself is approval-gated.\\n+\\n+#### Mental model\\n+\\n+Hold your work in JS: an array of items in, an array of results out. Merge each\\n+dispatch result back onto its item. Multi-stage analysis means: run a pass,\\n+filter or regroup the array in JS, then run another pass over the survivors.\\n+\\n+You can run the whole workflow in one `eval` call or split it across\\n+several — both are fine. A single end-to-end script (generate, compare, pick a\\n+winner; or review every item, then synthesize) is clean when you can write it\\n+in one go; splitting is also fine when you want to inspect results between\\n+stages. Either way, don't redo work across calls — reuse what is already in\\n+scope (see \\\"Reuse what earlier evals left in scope\\\" below).\\n+\\n+#### Fan out with bounded concurrency\\n+\\n+Dispatch independent work in parallel with `Promise.all`. Batches around 10 are\\n+a conservative recommendation, not a required limit; use larger batches when\\n+appropriate for the workload and its admission controls. The bridge enforces\\n+a per-REPL cap of 32 concurrent subagent calls; excess\\n+calls wait for capacity.\\n+\\n+```javascript\\n+const files = [\\\"/src/a.ts\\\", \\\"/src/b.ts\\\", \\\"/src/c.ts\\\"]; // found while exploring\\n+const batchSize = 10;\\n+const reviewed = [];\\n+for (let i = 0; i < files.length; i += batchSize) {\\n+  const batch = files.slice(i, i + batchSize);\\n+  reviewed.push(...(await Promise.all(batch.map(async (file) => {\\n+    const result = await task({\\n+      description: \\\"Read \\\" + file + \\\" and review it for SQL injection. \\\" +\\n+        \\\"Cite line numbers.\\\",\\n+      subagentType: \\\"reviewer\\\",\\n+      responseSchema: {\\n+        type: \\\"object\\\",\\n+        properties: {\\n+          vulnerabilities: {\\n+            type: \\\"array\\\",\\n+            items: {\\n+              type: \\\"object\\\",\\n+              properties: {\\n+                type: { type: \\\"string\\\" },\\n+                line: { type: \\\"number\\\" },\\n+                evidence: { type: \\\"string\\\" },\\n+              },\\n+              required: [\\\"type\\\", \\\"line\\\", \\\"evidence\\\"],\\n+            },\\n+          },\\n+        },\\n+        required: [\\\"vulnerabilities\\\"],\\n+      },\\n+    });\\n+    return { file, ...result };\\n+  }))));\\n+}\\n+```\\n+\\n+#### Explore with your own tools first, then distribute\\n+\\n+You already have your normal tools for reading, listing, globbing, and\\n+grepping files. Use them to explore and understand the task BEFORE you write\\n+the orchestration script. These are ordinary tool calls, separate from the\\n+`eval` tool: read the data file, list or glob the directory, grep for\\n+what matters, then decide how to split the work.\\n+\\n+Never write `eval` code that spawns a subagent just to read or parse a\\n+file or list a directory. That is a deterministic step you do yourself with a\\n+direct tool call; spending a whole agent loop on it is wasteful.\\n+\\n+Once you understand the shape of the work, you have creative freedom in how\\n+you split it:\\n+\\n+- One dispatch per file or per record, when the items are already separate.\\n+- Chunk a large input yourself — read it, split it, optionally write a small\\n+  input file per chunk — and dispatch one subagent per chunk.\\n+- A cheap classification pass first, then deeper dispatches only for the items\\n+  that warrant them.\\n+\\n+Then write JavaScript in the `eval` tool that distributes the heavy,\\n+agentic work to subagents with `task()`: analyzing file contents, exploring a\\n+codebase, making judgment calls, rewriting code, or synthesizing a report.\\n+\\n+Hand each subagent a locator, not a payload. Subagents have their own file\\n+tools, so for anything that lives in a file — a file to review, rewrite, or\\n+audit — pass the path and let the subagent read it. Do NOT read a whole file\\n+just to paste its contents into the description; that bloats every dispatch\\n+and duplicates the file across them. Reserve inline content for small or\\n+derived data that has no path of its own: a single parsed record, or a chunk\\n+you split out of a larger input (write the chunk to its own file and pass that\\n+path if it is large). Assemble the results in JS.\\n+\\n+#### Compose multiple stages\\n+\\n+Filter the array in JS between passes. For example: first ask subagents for a\\n+cheap classification, filter to the risky items, then dispatch deeper reviews\\n+only for those items.\\n+\\n+```javascript\\n+const tagged = await Promise.all(files.map((file) =>\\n+  task({\\n+    description: \\\"Read \\\" + file + \\\" and classify it as handler, util, \\\" +\\n+      \\\"test, or config.\\\",\\n+    subagentType: \\\"reviewer\\\",\\n+    responseSchema: {\\n+      type: \\\"object\\\",\\n+      properties: { kind: { type: \\\"string\\\" }, risky: { type: \\\"boolean\\\" } },\\n+      required: [\\\"kind\\\", \\\"risky\\\"],\\n+    },\\n+  }).then((tag) => ({ file, ...tag }))\\n+));\\n+\\n+const riskyHandlers = tagged.filter((it) => it.kind === \\\"handler\\\" && it.risky);\\n+const deepReviews = await Promise.all(riskyHandlers.map((it) =>\\n+  task({\\n+    description: \\\"Deep security review of \\\" + it.file + \\\". Cite line numbers.\\\",\\n+    subagentType: \\\"reviewer\\\",\\n+  }).then((review) => ({ ...it, review }))\\n+));\\n+```\\n+\\n+#### Return results via the last expression, not `console.log`\\n+\\n+The value of the last expression in an `eval` call (or a resolved\\n+top-level `await`) is returned to you as the result. Make that final\\n+expression the variable holding your result and read it from there.\\n+`console.log` is only for incidental debugging: its output is capped and\\n+truncated, while the returned value is not, so never `console.log` your\\n+actual results.\\n+\\n+Keep large intermediate sets in JS variables and return only a compact\\n+summary or a small slice, not the entire dataset. To persist full output,\\n+have a subagent write it, or write it with your own file tool outside the\\n+`eval` call.\\n+\\n+#### Reuse what earlier evals left in scope\\n+\\n+The REPL is persistent within a turn: every top-level variable, function, and\\n+class you declare is kept and is available in your next `eval` call\\n+(each is hoisted to global scope). So if a later step needs something an\\n+earlier eval produced or bound, **reference that variable by name** — do not\\n+write a new literal that re-types data a previous eval already returned or\\n+computed.\\n+\\n+If you catch yourself pasting a big array or object of values you produced in\\n+an earlier call, that is the tell: the variable is still in scope, so use it.\\n+Re-typing prior results as a fresh literal wastes tokens and drifts from what\\n+actually ran.\\n+\\n+```javascript\\n+// An earlier eval bound this:\\n+//   const auditResults = await Promise.all(files.map(/* ...audit... */));\\n+\\n+// A later eval — reference it; do NOT paste the findings back in as a literal:\\n+const findings = auditResults.flatMap((r) =>\\n+  r.findings.map((f) => ({ ...f, file: r.file }))\\n+);\\n+const verified = await Promise.all(findings.map((f) =>\\n+  task({\\n+    description: \\\"Verify this finding: \\\" + f.evidence,\\n+    subagentType: \\\"verifier\\\",\\n+  }).then((v) => ({ ...f, ...v }))\\n+));\\n+```\\n+\\n+#### When the user asks for a \\\"workflow\\\"\\n+\\n+If the user's request mentions running a \\\"workflow\\\" (or otherwise uses the\\n+word \\\"workflow\\\"), fan the work out to subagents rather than doing it all\\n+yourself. Explore with your own tools first as needed, then write JavaScript\\n+in the `eval` tool that dispatches subagents with `task()` and\\n+assembles their results. The point is to distribute the heavy work in\\n+parallel, not to grind through it one tool call at a time.\\n+\\n+\\n+### API Reference — `tools` namespace\\n+\\n+The agent tools listed below are exposed on the global object at `globalThis.tools` (also reachable as `tools`). It runs JavaScript in a persistent REPL.\\n+\\n+- State (variables, functions) persists across tool calls and across multiple turns for this conversation thread.\\n+- Top-level `await` works; Promises resolve before the call returns.\\n+- Runtime sandbox: no built-in filesystem, network, stdlib, or wall-clock APIs (`fetch`, `require`, `fs`, `process`, real `Date.now()` are unavailable or stubbed).\\n+- External side effects from inside the REPL are only reachable via the `tools.*` namespace documented in the API reference below.\\n+- Timeout: 5.0s per call. Memory: 64 MB total.\\n+- `console.log` output is captured and returned alongside the result.\\n+\\n+### Dispatching Subagents with `task`\\n+\\n+`task` is your primitive for running configured subagents from inside the\\n+JavaScript REPL. Your job here is to DISTRIBUTE work, not to do it yourself:\\n+write JavaScript that fans work out to subagents and assembles their results.\\n+You handle the orchestration - fan-out, filtering, deduplication, multi-stage\\n+flow, and synthesis - in plain JavaScript.\\n+\\n+#### The primitive\\n+\\n+```javascript\\n+await task({\\n+  description,      // full autonomous task prompt\\n+  subagentType,     // configured subagent name\\n+  label,            // optional short UI label for this dispatch\\n+  responseSchema,   // optional JSON Schema for structured output\\n+}); // -> Promise<unknown>\\n+```\\n+\\n+`task` runs a full agentic loop for the selected configured subagent. The\\n+subagent can use whatever tools it was configured with, iterate, inspect\\n+context, and return one final result. `subagentType` is required; use one of\\n+the configured subagent names.\\n+\\n+`description` is the only prompt the subagent receives for this dispatch. Make\\n+it complete: the goal, the constraints, what to inspect, and the exact shape\\n+or level of detail you expect back. Give context as locators — file paths and\\n+symbol names — not as pasted file contents. If you already read a file while\\n+exploring, still pass its path and let the subagent read it; do not paste back\\n+what you read. Each dispatch is stateless from the caller's perspective; you\\n+cannot send follow-up messages to the same subagent run.\\n+\\n+`label` is optional: when provided, it is shown in the live progress UI\\n+instead of the default description-derived fallback. It is not sent to the\\n+subagent and does not affect execution.\\n+\\n+`responseSchema` is optional, but set it on any dispatch whose result feeds\\n+later code. A deterministic, typed shape is what lets you compose the next\\n+stage reliably — index it, sort it, compare fields, branch on it, merge it —\\n+instead of parsing free-form text. This is what makes a whole workflow\\n+composable as one script. When provided, the resolved value is already a typed\\n+JavaScript value matching the schema; do not call `JSON.parse` unless the\\n+subagent intentionally returned a JSON string. Subagents have their own file\\n+tools, so for anything that lives in a file — a file to review, rewrite, or\\n+audit — pass the path and let the subagent read it. Do NOT read a whole file\\n+just to paste its contents into the description; that bloats every dispatch\\n+and duplicates the file across them. Reserve inline content for small or\\n+derived data that has no path of its own: a single parsed record, or a chunk\\n+you split out of a larger input (write the chunk to its own file and pass that\\n+path if it is large). Assemble the results in JS.\\n+\\n+#### Compose multiple stages\\n+\\n+Filter the array in JS between passes. For example: first ask subagents for a\\n+cheap classification, filter to the risky items, then dispatch deeper reviews\\n+only for those items.\\n+\\n+```javascript\\n+const tagged = await Promise.all(files.map((file) =>\\n+  task({\\n+    description: \\\"Read \\\" + file + \\\" and classify it as handler, util, \\\" +\\n+      \\\"test, or config.\\\",\\n+    subagentType: \\\"reviewer\\\",\\n+    responseSchema: {\\n+      type: \\\"object\\\",\\n+      properties: { kind: { type: \\\"string\\\" }, risky: { type: \\\"boolean\\\" } },\\n+      required: [\\\"kind\\\", \\\"risky\\\"],\\n+    },\\n+  }).then((tag) => ({ file, ...tag }))\\n+));\\n+\\n+const riskyHandlers = tagged.filter((it) => it.kind === \\\"handler\\\" && it.risky);\\n+const deepReviews = await Promise.all(riskyHandlers.map((it) =>\\n+  task({\\n+    description: \\\"Deep security review of \\\" + it.file + \\\". Cite line numbers.\\\",\\n+    subagentType: \\\"reviewer\\\",\\n+  }).then((review) => ({ ...it, review }))\\n+));\\n+```\\n+\\n+#### Return results via the last expression, not `console.log`\\n+\\n+The value of the last expression in an `eval` call (or a resolved\\n+top-level `await`) is returned to you as the result. Make that final\\n+expression the variable holding your result and read it from there.\\n+`console.log` is only for incidental debugging: its output is capped and\\n+truncated, while the returned value is not, so never `console.log` your\\n+actual results.\\n+\\n+Keep large intermediate sets in JS variables and return only a compact\\n+summary or a small slice, not the entire dataset. To persist full output,\\n+have a subagent write it, or write it with your own file tool outside the\\n+`eval` call.\\n+\\n+#### Reuse what earlier evals left in scope\\n+\\n+The REPL is persistent within a turn: every top-level variable, function, and\\n+class you declare is kept and is available in your next `eval` call\\n+(each is hoisted to global scope). So if a later step needs something an\\n+earlier eval produced or bound, **reference that variable by name** — do not\\n+write a new literal that re-types data a previous eval already returned or\\n+computed.\\n+\\n+If you catch yourself pasting a big array or object of values you produced in\\n+an earlier call, that is the tell: the variable is still in scope, so use it.\\n+Re-typing prior results as a fresh literal wastes tokens and drifts from what\\n+actually ran.\\n+\\n+```javascript\\n+// An earlier eval bound this:\\n+//   const auditResults = await Promise.all(files.map(/* ...audit... */));\\n+\\n+// A later eval — reference it; do NOT paste the findings back in as a literal:\\n+const findings = auditResults.flatMap((r) =>\\n+  r.findings.map((f) => ({ ...f, file: r.file }))\\n+);\\n+const verified = await Promise.all(findings.map((f) =>\\n+  task({\\n+    description: \\\"Verify this finding: \\\" + f.evidence,\\n+    subagentType: \\\"verifier\\\",\\n+  }).then((v) => ({ ...f, ...v }))\\n+));\\n+```\\n+\\n+#### When the user asks for a \\\"workflow\\\"\\n+\\n+If the user's request mentions running a \\\"workflow\\\" (or otherwise uses the\\n+word \\\"workflow\\\"), fan the work out to subagents rather than doing it all\\n+yourself. Explore with your own tools first as needed, then write JavaScript\\n+in the `eval` tool that dispatches subagents with `task()` and\\n+assembles their results. The point is to distribute the heavy work in\\n+parallel, not to grind through it one tool call at a time.\\n+\\n+\\n+### API Reference — `tools` namespace\\n+\\n+The agent tools listed below are exposed on the global object at `globalThis.tools` (also reachable as `tools`). Each takes a single object argument and returns a Promise that resolves to the tool's native value: strings as strings, numbers as numbers, lists as arrays, dicts as objects, and `None` as `null`. You do NOT need to `JSON.parse` results — they are already typed.\\n+\\n+Invocation pattern: `await tools.<name>({ ... })`.\\n+\\n+- Use `await` to get tool results; combine with `Promise.all` for independent calls so they run concurrently.\\n+- If the task needs multiple tool calls, prefer one `eval` invocation that performs all of them rather than splitting the work across multiple `eval` calls — each round-trip costs a model turn.\\n+- Pipeline dependent calls within a single program. If a result from one tool is needed as input to a later tool, chain them in one program instead of returning the intermediate value to the model.\\n+- If a tool returns an ID or other value that can be passed directly into the next tool, trust it and chain the calls instead of stopping to double-check it.\\n+- To inspect an intermediate value, `console.log` it inside the same program; otherwise, fetch as much information as possible in one call.\\n+- Only split work across multiple `eval` invocations when you genuinely cannot determine what to do next without additional model reasoning or user input.\\n+\\n+Example shape — substitute real tool names:\\n+\\n+```typescript\\n+const users = await tools.findUsers({ name: \\\"Ada\\\" });\\n+const userId = users[0].id;\\n+const [city, normalized] = await Promise.all([\\n+  tools.cityForUser({ user_id: userId }),\\n+  tools.normalize({ name: \\\"Ada\\\" }),\\n+]);\\n+console.log({ city, normalized });\\n+```\\n+\\n+```typescript\\n+/** Create or update customers. */\\n+tools.upsertCustomers(input: {\\n+  customers: { name: string; address: { city: string; postal_code: string }; billing_address?: { city: string; postal_code: string } | null; tags?: Record<string, string> }[];\\n+}): Promise<{ name: string; address: { city: string; postal_code: string }; billing_address?: { city: string; postal_code: string } | null; tags?: Record<string, string> }[]>\\n+\\n+/** Get the org tree under a unit. */\\n+tools.getOrgTree(input: {\\n+  root: string;\\n+}): Promise<{ name: string; children?: unknown[] }>\\n+```\"},{\"sha\":\"fd6dce4f9ab54e76ed36deb94beec3e7a352b9a7\",\"filename\":\"libs/partners/quickjs/tests/unit_tests/smoke_tests/test_system_prompt.py\",\"status\":\"modified\",\"additions\":58,\"deletions\":1,\"changes\":59,\"blob_url\":\"https://github.com/langchain-ai/deepagents/blob/5829691de8f43d201f9534fb731643223c0bbccc/libs%2Fpartners%2Fquickjs%2Ftests%2Funit_tests%2Fsmoke_tests%2Ftest_system_prompt.py\",\"raw_url\":\"https://github.com/langchain-ai/deepagents/raw/5829691de8f43d201f9534fb731643223c0bbccc/libs%2Fpartners%2Fquickjs%2Ftests%2Funit_tests%2Fsmoke_tests%2Ftest_system_prompt.py\",\"contents_url\":\"https://api.github.com/repos/langchain-ai/deepagents/contents/libs%2Fpartners%2Fquickjs%2Ftests%2Funit_tests%2Fsmoke_tests%2Ftest_system_prompt.py?ref=5829691de8f43d201f9534fb731643223c0bbccc\",\"patch\":\"@@ The remaining 11 production lines record the measured draft and its invalidation lifecycle.\\n\\nThe 107-line regression allocation is required to protect zero repeated scrollHeight reads plus shrinking, equal-length replacement and scheduled cap changes. Both capped-input regressions fail on main (four reads) and pass with the fix (zero); all 66 focused tests, touched-file format/lint pass, and final committed-range P0-P2 autoreview is scoped-clean. All product, UI/browser, type, lint and security CI passed. The inherited test-line guard remains 8 lines over its funded ceiling; a pinned-main Crabbox replay also fails that guard. The PR funds exactly its 107-line growth, with no shared-baseline increase. Landing uses the native pre-existing-failure evidence route.\\n\\nSupersedes #154272, thanks @alfredjbclaw. data->>'taskId'=$3 ORDER BY updated_at DESC,id\",\n      [owner, kind, taskId],\n    );\n    return result.rows.map((row) => row.data as T);\n  }\n  /** Rows of one kind named by id, in the same order `list` returns them. */\n  async listByIds<T = Record<string, unknown>>(\n    owner: string,\n    kind: string,\n    ids: readonly string[],\n  ): Promise<T[]> {\n    if (ids.length === 0) return [];\n    const result = await this.db.query(\n      \"SELECT data FROM records WHERE owner=$1 AND kind=$2 AND id=ANY($3) ORDER BY updated_at DESC,id\",\n      [owner, kind, [...ids]],\n    );\n    return result.rows.map((row) => row.data as T);\n  }\n  async listByStatus<T = Record<string, unknown>>(\n    owner: string,\n    kind: string,\n    status: string,\n  ): Promise<T[]> {\n    const result = await this.db.query(\n      \"SELECT data FROM records WHERE owner=$1 AND kind=$2 AND data->>'status'=$3 ORDER BY updated_at DESC,id\",\n      [owner, kind, status],\n    );\n    return result.rows.map((row) => row.data as T);\n  }\n  async put<T extends { id: string }>(owner: string, kind: string, value: T): Promise<T> {\n    await this.db.query(\n      \"INSERT INTO records(owner,kind,id,data) VALUES($1,$2,$3,$4::jsonb) ON CONFLICT(owner,kind,id) DO UPDATE SET data=excluded.data,updated_at=now()\",\n      [owner, kind, value.id, JSON.stringify(value)],\n    );\n    return value;\n  }\n  async remove(owner: string, kind: string, id: string): Promise<void> {\n    await this.db.query(\"DELETE FROM records WHERE owner=$1 AND kind=$2 AND id=$3\", [\n      owner,\n      kind,\n      id,\n    ]);\n  }\n  async compareAndSwap<T>(\n    owner: string,\n    kind: string,\n    id: string,\n    expected: Record<string, unknown>,\n    patch: Record<string, unknown>,\n  ): Promise<T | null> {\n    const result = await this.db.query(\n      \"UPDATE records SET data=data || $5::jsonb,updated_at=now() WHERE owner=$1 AND kind=$2 AND id=$3 AND data @> $4::jsonb RETURNING data\",\n      [owner, kind, id, JSON.stringify(expected), JSON.stringify(patch)],\n    );\n    return (result.rows[0]?.data as T | undefined) ?? null;\n  }\n  // Update only the selected checkbox against the current row, preserving concurrent\n  // additions, renames, reordering and other milestones' completion state.\n  async setMilestoneDone<T>(owner: string, goalId: string, milestoneId: string, done: boolean) {\n    const result = await this.db.query(\n      `UPDATE records SET data=jsonb_set(data, '{milestones}', (\n        SELECT jsonb_agg(CASE WHEN item->>'id'=$3\n          THEN item || jsonb_build_object('done', $4::boolean) ELSE item END ORDER BY ordinal)\n        FROM jsonb_array_elements(data->'milestones') WITH ORDINALITY AS milestones(item, ordinal)\n      )), updated_at=now()\n      WHERE owner=$1 AND kind='goals' AND id=$2\n        AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM jsonb_array_elements(data->'milestones') item WHERE item->>'id'=$3)\n      RETURNING data`,\n      [owner, goalId, milestoneId, done],\n    );\n    return (result.rows[0]?.data as T | undefined) ?? null;\n  }\n  async insertIfAbsent<T extends { id: string }>(\n    owner: string,\n    kind: string,\n    value: T,\n  ): Promise<T | null> {\n    const result = await this.db.query(\n      \"INSERT INTO records(owner,kind,id,data) VALUES($1,$2,$3,$4::jsonb) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING data\",\n      [owner, kind, value.id, JSON.stringify(value)],\n    );\n    return (result.rows[0]?.data as T | undefined) ?? null;\n  }\n  async scan<T>(kind: string): Promise<{ owner: string; value: T }[]> {\n    const result = await this.db.query(\n      \"SELECT jsonb_build_object('owner',owner,'value',data) AS data FROM records WHERE kind=$1 ORDER BY updated_at ASC\",\n      [kind],\n    );\n    return result.rows.map((row) => row.data as { owner: string; value: T });\n  }\n  async claim<T>(owner: string, id: string, status: string, now: string): Promise<T | null> {\n    const result = await this.db.query(\n      `UPDATE records AS action SET data=jsonb_set(data,'{status}',$4::jsonb),updated_at=now()\n       WHERE owner=$1 AND kind='actions' AND id=$2 AND data->>'status'='awaiting_review'\n       AND (data->>'expiresAt')::timestamptz>$3::timestamptz\n       AND ($4::jsonb <> '\"executing\"'::jsonb OR data->>'taskId' IS NULL OR EXISTS (\n         SELECT 1 FROM records task WHERE task.owner=action.owner AND task.kind='tasks'\n         AND task.id=action.data->>'taskId' AND task.data->>'status' IN ('running','waiting_approval')\n       )) RETURNING data`,\n      [owner, id, now, JSON.stringify(status)],\n    );\n    return (result.rows[0]?.data as T | undefined) ?? null;\n  }\n  async recoverInterruptedActions(): Promise<void> {\n    await this.db.query(\n      `UPDATE records SET data=data || '{\"status\":\"outcome_unknown\",\"error\":\"Server restarted during execution. Check the provider before creating another action.\"}'::jsonb WHERE kind='actions' AND data->>'status'='executing'`,\n    );\n  }\n  async take<T>(owner: string, kind: string, id: string): Promise<T | null> {\n    const result = await this.db.query(\n      \"DELETE FROM records WHERE owner=$1 AND kind=$2 AND id=$3 RETURNING data\",\n      [owner, kind, id],\n    );\n    return (result.rows[0]?.data as T | undefined) ?? null;\n  }\n  close(): Promise<void> {\n    return this.db.close();\n  }\n  async updateCredential(owner: string, connectionId: string, secret: string): Promise<boolean> {\n    const result = await this.db.query(\n      \"UPDATE records SET data=jsonb_set(data,'{secret}',$3::jsonb),updated_at=now() WHERE owner=$1 AND kind='credentials' AND id='google' AND data->>'connectionId'=$2 RETURNING data\",\n      [owner, connectionId, JSON.stringify(secret)],\n    );\n    return result.rows.length === 1;\n  }\n}\n\n/** Idle clients can be disconnected by a database restart; without a listener pg's `error` event crashes the process. */\nexport function createPool(connectionString: string) {\n  const pool = new pg.Pool({ connectionString, max: 5 });\n  pool.on(\"error\", (error) => backgroundFailure(\"postgres pool\", error));\n  return pool;\n}\n\nexport async function createStore(\n  options: { dataDir?: string; databaseUrl?: string } = {},\n): Promise<Store> {\n  let database: Database;\n  if (options.databaseUrl) {\n    const pool = createPool(options.databaseUrl);\n    database = { query: async (sql, params) => pool.query(sql, params), close: () => pool.end() };\n  } else {\n    if (options.dataDir) await mkdir(dirname(options.dataDir), { recursive: true, mode: 0o700 });\n    const embedded = new PGlite(options.dataDir);\n    await embedded.waitReady;\n    database = {\n      query: (sql, params) => embedded.query<Row>(sql, params),\n      close: () => embedded.close(),\n    };\n  }\n  await database.query(\n    \"CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS records(owner text NOT NULL,kind text NOT NULL,id text NOT NULL,data jsonb NOT NULL,updated_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),PRIMARY KEY(owner,kind,id))\",\n  );\n  return new Store(database);\n}\n","display_url":"https://github.com/CopilotKit/openmuse/blob/a4944f4c471d3dc93b8bfc060b5da309b5216ab2/apps/server/src/db.ts"}}
